rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-footprints-wi.title: Footprints without Feet — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-footprints-wi.subtitle: Muddy footprints appear on a London street — but nobody is there. H. G. Wells's invisible scientist, explained

sections.md:
Two boys in a London square stop and stare. On the steps of a house, **fresh muddy footprints** are appearing, one after another — *as if someone were walking* — yet there is **no one there**. The boys follow the prints down the street until they grow fainter and vanish.

This eerie scene opens *Footprints without Feet*, adapted from **The Invisible Man** (1897) by **H. G. Wells** (1866–1946), the English writer often called a father of **science fiction**. Wells also wrote *The Time Machine* and *The War of the Worlds*.

The chapter follows **Griffin**, a brilliant scientist who discovers how to make the human body **invisible**. But invisibility doesn't make him happy or powerful — it makes him **lawless, lonely and hunted**.

**Big idea:** science without ethics can turn genius into a menace.
keyTerms: science fiction — stories based on imagined scientific discoveries
invisible — cannot be seen
lawless — not obeying laws

sections.h: Griffin's discovery — and the science behind invisibility
sections.md:
**Griffin** is a scientist who has discovered a way to make the human body **transparent**. He swallows certain rare drugs, and his body becomes as transparent as a sheet of glass, though it remains as solid as glass too — he can be touched but not seen.

**How would that work, really?** We see objects because they **absorb, reflect or refract light**. Glass is almost invisible in water because light passes through and bends very little. For a body to be invisible, every tissue would need to have the same **refractive index** as air and absorb no light. Wells hand-waves the chemistry — that is the 'fiction' part — but the idea is based on real optics. (A fun puzzle: a fully invisible person would also be **blind**, since the retina must absorb light to see! Wells doesn't deal with this.)

**Important limits in the story:**
- He is **invisible only when naked**. Clothes, food in his stomach, and mud on his feet are visible.
- So he must go about **without clothes**, even in the **cold of a London winter** — he catches a chill and sneezes.
- That's why the boys see the **muddy footprints**: his feet, freshly washed in a puddle? — no, they are footprints because he has just stepped in mud, and the mud stays visible.

sections.h: London: fire, a cold winter and a department store
sections.md:
Griffin, a **rather unscrupulous** man, had been living in London. He had quarrelled with his **landlord**, who wanted to turn him out of his room. In revenge, Griffin **set fire to the house**, and to escape, he took off his clothes and became invisible.

Now he was **homeless**, without clothes, without money, invisible but **freezing** in the London winter.

He slipped into a big **London store** for warmth. When the store closed, he broke open boxes and wrapped himself in warm clothes. He found food in the store's kitchens and slept on a pile of quilts. Next morning, the assistants came in and found him — or rather, a fully dressed figure. Griffin panicked, threw off the clothes, and escaped by becoming invisible again, **stark naked** in the cold once more.

Next he went to a **theatrical company's shop** in **Drury Lane** (London's theatre district). There he found a **false nose**, **dark glasses**, **bandages**, **whiskers** and a **wide-brimmed hat**, so that he could appear in public without revealing his invisibility. To escape, he **attacked the shopkeeper from behind** and robbed him of all the money he could find.

**Character note:** Griffin's actions are increasingly **criminal**: arson, theft, assault. His brilliance as a scientist is not matched by any sense of right and wrong.

check.q: Why did Griffin set fire to his landlord's house?
options: In revenge, because the landlord wanted to turn him out
check.why: Griffin was angry that the landlord wanted to evict him, so he set fire to the house and escaped invisible.

sections.h: Iping: the strange guest at the Coach and Horses
sections.md:
Wanting peace to work on a way to become **visible** again, Griffin travels to the village of **Iping** and takes two rooms at the local inn, the **Coach and Horses**. It is the off-season, and the landlady, **Mrs Hall**, is delighted to have a guest in winter — especially one who pays in advance.

But the guest is **very strange**:
- His head is entirely covered in **bandages**; he wears dark glasses and a false nose.
- He wears **gloves** even indoors.
- He has **whiskers** and a wide hat.
- He keeps to his rooms, works with bottles and chemicals, and is **rude and bad-tempered**.

Mrs Hall, being curious and friendly, tries to chat with him; he snaps at her. She tells the villagers she thinks he has had an accident that disfigured him. The villagers make guesses: a criminal hiding from police? A man with a terrible face? He is the talk of Iping.

**The comic tone:** Wells writes these village scenes with gentle humour — gossip, curiosity and misunderstanding.

options: It was the off-season and he paid in advance
He promised to fix the inn
check.why: Guests were rare in winter, and the stranger paid in advance, so Mrs Hall was glad to have him.

sections.h: The clergyman's study and the burglary
sections.md:
Soon, **strange things** start happening in Iping. Early one morning, the **clergyman** and his wife are woken by noises in the study. They creep downstairs and hear the **chink of money** being taken from the clergyman's desk. They burst into the study, poker in hand — but there is **no one**. The desk drawer is open, the money is gone, but the room is empty. The clergyman's wife is certain she heard someone **sneeze** in the hallway.

At the same time, **Mr and Mrs Hall** find the stranger's door open and his room **empty** — but his clothes and bandages are lying about! How could he have gone out without clothes? As Mrs Hall stares, the **bed-clothes** gather themselves into a bundle and leap over the bed rail; the stranger's **hat** jumps off the bedpost and flies at her face; the **bedroom chair** springs into the air and charges at her, pushing the Halls out of the room, and the door slams and locks.

Mrs Hall is convinced the room is **haunted** — that the stranger has put **spirits** into her furniture. *My poor dear mother's chair!* she cries.

**Humour and horror mix** here: scary events described through a landlady's fussy concern for her furniture.

check.q: What did Mrs Hall believe after the furniture attacked her?
options: That the stranger was a magician
That the stranger had put spirits into her furniture
That her husband was playing a trick
check.why: Unable to explain the flying hat and charging chair, Mrs Hall believed the stranger had bewitched the furniture with spirits.

sections.h: Unmasked: the fight and the escape
sections.md:
When the stranger reappears, the villagers want an explanation. Mrs Hall confronts him, demanding to know why he went out and how he entered his room without passing through the door. He becomes furious and does something astonishing: he **removes his bandages, glasses and nose**, revealing — **nothing**. A **headless figure** in clothes stands before them!

The people in the bar **scream** and rush out into the street.

The village **constable**, **Jaffers**, arrives with a warrant to arrest the stranger for the clergyman's robbery. He tries to seize him — and finds he is grappling with a **headless man** who keeps on fighting. Jaffers holds on to the invisible wrist. Then the stranger starts taking off his clothes. A shirt flies off; the figure becomes **completely invisible**. People feel blows from an invisible fist; Jaffers is struck and knocked unconscious? — he is knocked down, and Griffin **escapes**, free and unseen.

**Ending meaning:** Griffin's invisibility gives him escape but not peace. He is a fugitive, hunted, hated and alone.

sections.md:
**Griffin — character sketch:**
- **Brilliant** scientist who achieved what no one had.
- **Unscrupulous** and **lawless** — arson, theft, assault.
- **Rude, ill-tempered**, secretive.
- **Lonely** — invisibility cuts him off from humanity.

**Themes:**
1. **Misuse of science.** Knowledge without moral responsibility leads to harm.
2. **Power corrupts.** Invisibility feels like power, but Griffin uses it for crime.
3. **Isolation.** Being unseen means being unknown and unloved.
4. **Curiosity and gossip** in village life (the comic side).

**Science-fiction features:** a scientific idea (invisibility) explored seriously; its realistic limitations (naked in winter, visible mud, visible food); consequences for society.

**Language corner:** words — *unscrupulous, eccentric, fugitive, warrant, constable, clergyman*. Notice the **passive voice** in reporting events (*The money was taken*), and **verbs of motion** for invisible actions (*the chair sprang, the hat leapt*) — a clever technique to show an invisible actor.

rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-making-scient.title: The Making of a Scientist — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-making-scient.subtitle: A boy who collected butterflies, a book from his mother, a failed science fair — and a discovery about how cells read DNA

sections.h: A hook: from butterfly net to the cover of a journal
sections.md:
At twenty-two, **Richard H. Ebright** was a co-author (with a college room-mate) of a scientific paper that appeared in *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* (1979), proposing a new theory about how cells read their genetic blueprint. How did a boy from a small town in **Pennsylvania**, USA, get there?

The answer begins with **butterflies**.

*The Making of a Scientist* by **Robert W. Peterson** is a short biographical piece about Ebright. It shows the ingredients that make a scientist: **curiosity**, **hard work**, a supportive **mother**, encouraging **teachers**, learning from **failure**, and a spirit of **competition** to do one's best.

The chapter is in the supplementary reader **Footprints without Feet**.
keyTerms: biography — a life story written by someone else
curiosity — desire to know and learn
DNA — molecule carrying genetic instructions

sections.md:
Ebright grew up in **Reading, Pennsylvania**. He was an only child, and there wasn't much to do for fun there. So he **collected things** — anything he could find:

- **butterflies** (he collected all twenty-five species found around his hometown),
- **rocks and fossils**,
- **coins**,
- and he was an eager **astronomer**, studying the stars at night.

He was also a keen student, getting good marks at school.

His **mother** was his greatest support. His father died when Richard was in the **third grade**. His mother took him on trips, bought him **telescopes, microscopes, cameras, mounting materials** and other equipment, and helped him in every way. She was his **only companion** in the early years; at night she gave him **learning tasks**. If he didn't have anything to do, she found something for him to learn.

**Lesson:** a curious child flourishes with encouragement and resources at home. Ebright's mother didn't push grades — she fed curiosity.

check.q: Who encouraged Ebright most in his early years?
check.why: After his father's death, his mother bought him equipment, took him on trips and set learning tasks, encouraging his curiosity.

sections.h: The book that changed his life: Travels of Monarch X
sections.md:
The turning point came when his mother gave him a children's book called **The Travels of Monarch X**. It described how **monarch butterflies** migrate to **Central America** (Mexico). The book offered readers a chance to help: tag butterflies to help **Dr Frederick A. Urquhart** of the **University of Toronto** study their migration.

Ebright's mother wrote to Dr Urquhart, and Richard began **tagging** monarchs — placing small labels on their wings so that, if found far away, they could be traced. The experiment opened **the world of science** to him.

At first, catching butterflies was slow, so Ebright started **raising** them. He would catch a female, collect her eggs, and raise the caterpillars in his basement, through the **pupa** stage to adult butterflies. He then tagged them and let them fly. He estimates he tagged thousands.

After a while, the tagging became boring: few butterflies were recaptured — he got only **two** recaptured, and they had been found no farther than 75 miles away. But his interest in the **monarch's life cycle** had been fired.

check.why: His mother gave him The Travels of Monarch X, which led him to tag monarchs for Dr Urquhart and opened up science to him.

sections.h: Failure at the science fair — and a lesson
sections.md:
In **seventh grade**, Ebright entered a county **science fair** with slides of frog tissues under a microscope — and **lost**. The winners had done real **experiments**; he had only made a neat display.

He realised the difference between **displaying** knowledge and **discovering** something. Science means asking a question and testing it.

So in **eighth grade** he did a real project: he tried to find the cause of a viral disease that kills nearly all monarch caterpillars every few years. He thought it might be carried by a beetle. He tried raising caterpillars in the presence of beetles. He didn't get any real results, but he showed his experiments and **won**.

The next year he did a project testing the theory that **viceroy butterflies** copy **monarchs**. Viceroys look very similar to monarchs. Birds avoid monarchs because they taste bad (monarch caterpillars feed on milkweed, which makes them unpalatable). So by looking like monarchs, viceroys are protected — this is called **mimicry**. Ebright fed viceroys and monarchs to birds and found that a starling would eat ordinary bird food, and would eat viceroys too… but not monarchs, which supported the theory? The textbook records that his project, which showed birds might avoid both, won **zoology** honours at the county fair.

**Lesson:** failure taught him to design proper experiments.

check.q: What lesson did Ebright learn from losing the seventh-grade science fair?
options: Neat displays are not enough — real experiments are needed
check.why: He saw that winners had done genuine experiments, so he shifted from showing slides to testing questions.

sections.h: The gold spots and the hormone
sections.md:
Ebright's most famous school project came in **high school**. He studied the **twelve tiny gold spots** on the **monarch pupa** (chrysalis). Everyone assumed they were just ornamental. Ebright wondered: *what are they for?*

He built a **mechanism** to study them. He found that the gold spots produce a **hormone** needed for the butterfly's full development. This idea won him **first place** in the county science fair and gave him the chance to go to the **International Science and Engineering Fair**, where he won **third place** for zoology.

He also got to work during the summer at the **Walter Reed Army Institute of Research** in a laboratory, and later at the **US Department of Agriculture** in the entomology (insect) lab. He went on to Harvard University.

In his senior year of high school, he went further: he grew **cells from a monarch's wing** in a culture and showed that the cells would divide and develop into normal butterfly wing scales only if they were fed the hormone from the gold spots. That project won **first place** for zoology at the International Science Fair and a trip to the army's labs.

**From butterflies to DNA:** at college (Harvard), Ebright and his room-mate **James R. Wong** worked on the chemical structure of the hormone. Looking at an X-ray photo of it, Ebright suddenly had an idea about how cells read the 'blueprint' in their **DNA** — the substance in the nucleus that controls heredity. They published the theory. It was a big step toward understanding life, and possibly diseases like **cancer**.

sections.h: More than a scientist: qualities and teachers
sections.md:
Ebright was not only a scientist. He was a champion **debater**, a public speaker, a good **canoeist** and an all-round outdoors person. He was also an expert **photographer**, particularly of nature and scientific exhibits.

His **social studies teacher**, **Richard A. Weiherer**, said that Richard was always looking for a better way to do things, and that he wanted to **win** — not to beat others, but to do his best. He had a **competitive spirit** in the healthiest sense.

**What makes a scientist (according to the chapter)?**

| Ingredient | Example from Ebright's life |
|---|---|
| A first-rate mind | Top student, quick to grasp ideas |
| Curiosity | Questioned the purpose of gold spots |
| The will to win for the right reasons | Did his best, not just to defeat others |
| Support | Mother, Dr Urquhart, teachers |
| Learning from failure | Seventh-grade fair loss → real experiments |
| Hard work | Raised thousands of butterflies |

Today Ebright is a molecular biologist known for research on bacterial **RNA polymerase** (the enzyme that reads DNA) and for speaking on laboratory safety and science policy.

check.q: According to his teacher, why did Ebright want to win?
options: To do his best, for the right reasons
check.why: Weiherer noted that Ebright's competitive spirit was about doing his best, not merely defeating others.

parts.md: Tanvi, in Class 9 in Nashik, noticed odd silver squiggles on the mango leaves in her school garden. Her science teacher said, 'Don't just photograph them — ask a question.' Tanvi asked: are the squiggles more common on sunny or shady branches? Every week she counted squiggles on twenty leaves from each side.

Her first chart at the district science fair lost to a working model of a water purifier. The judge told her, 'Good counting — but what's making the squiggles?' Next year she raised the tiny larvae in jars, identified them as leaf-mining insects with help from a college professor, and tested whether neem spray kept them away. She won. Like Ebright, she had learned the difference between showing and finding out.

Discovered the twelve gold spots on the monarch pupa produce a hormone needed for development.
Won top prizes at county and international science fairs; worked at Walter Reed and the US Department of Agriculture labs.
At Harvard, with James R. Wong, proposed a theory of how cells read DNA.
Qualities of a scientist: first-rate mind, curiosity, will to win for the right reasons, hard work.

rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-midnight-visi.title: The Midnight Visitor — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-midnight-visi.subtitle: A fat, unglamorous secret agent, a rival with a pistol, and a balcony that was never there

sections.h: A hook: what does a real spy look like?
sections.md:
Close your eyes and imagine a secret agent. You probably see someone tall, handsome and athletic, in a sharp suit, leaping across rooftops, a pistol in one hand and a coded message in the other. Films have trained us to expect this picture.

Now meet **Ausable**. He is fat. He is sloppy. Though he has lived in France for many years, he still speaks with a heavy American accent. He lives in a small, musty room at the top of a shabby French hotel. He does not climb walls or fight with his fists. And yet, by the end of a short evening, he defeats an armed enemy without lifting a finger.

*The Midnight Visitor* is a story by **Robert Arthur** (1909–1969), an American writer best known for mystery and suspense — radio plays, magazine stories and the *Three Investigators* series for young readers. Because the author died after 1965, his story is still under copyright, so this companion **does not reproduce the text**. Instead it gives you a full scene-by-scene retelling in our own words, explanations, character sketches, themes, language work and exam practice. Read the original in your *Footprints without Feet* book or in the free official PDF linked at the end.

**Why this story is in your book.** It is short, gripping and perfectly built: every detail placed early in the story is used later. It teaches you how writers create **suspense**, how they play with **reader expectations**, and how a **twist ending** works. Above all, its message is clear and timeless: **brains beat brawn**, and **appearances can be deceptive**.
keyTerms: secret agent — a spy working for a government
twist ending — a surprising, unexpected conclusion that changes how we see earlier events
presence of mind — the ability to think quickly and calmly in a crisis
suspense — the anxious curiosity a reader feels about what will happen next

sections.h: Scene 1 — Fowler meets a very ordinary spy
sections.md:
The story opens with a contrast. **Fowler** is a young writer who has managed to get an introduction to Ausable, a real secret agent. Fowler hopes to gather material for his writing: he dreams of the 'romance' of spying — mysterious women with dark eyes, whispered secrets in dim corridors, a midnight rendezvous, perhaps a gunshot.

What he actually gets is an evening that disappoints him at every step. Ausable is not dashing. He is so fat that he moves heavily and breathes loudly on the stairs. The two men had spent the evening at a dull French music hall, and now they climb the dim stairs of the hotel to Ausable's room on the **sixth (top) floor**. The corridor is dark and the hotel is drab.

As they walk, Ausable tells Fowler something to keep him interested: that night he expects an important paper to reach him — a report connected with some **new missiles**, a paper that many people would risk their lives for. Ausable mentions it in a calm, business-like way, as if he were talking about the weather. Fowler's excitement returns a little; perhaps there will be adventure after all.

**How the writer builds this scene.** Robert Arthur deliberately makes Ausable *look* unimpressive. This lowers both Fowler's and our expectations, so that his cleverness later will strike us with full force. The writer also slips in small facts that will matter later: the room is on the **sixth floor**, and Ausable is a man who arranges things in advance.

check.q: Why was Fowler disappointed in Ausable at first?
options: Ausable did not look or live like the glamorous spies Fowler had imagined
check.why: Fowler expected a dashing, mysterious spy, but Ausable was fat, ordinary, spoke with an American accent and lived in a shabby top-floor room — far from the romantic image.

sections.h: Scene 2 — The man with the pistol
sections.md:
Ausable unlocks the door and switches on the light. Fowler stops in shock. Standing in the room, facing them, is a man holding a **small automatic pistol**. This is **Max**, a rival agent. He is slim, smooth and confident, with a thin, unpleasant smile — exactly the kind of spy Fowler had been imagining.

Max has come for the missile report. He intends to wait until it is delivered and then take it, with the pistol making sure no one argues.

Fowler is thrilled and frightened at once. At last, here is danger! But Ausable's reaction is surprising: he does not panic, beg or shout. He looks **mildly annoyed**, as if Max were an inconvenient guest who had arrived uninvited. He remarks that he had thought Max was somewhere else (in Berlin, in Ausable's words). He speaks to Max almost conversationally.

**Key point for exams:** Ausable's calmness is his first weapon. A frightened man cannot think; a calm one can. By staying composed, Ausable keeps control of the conversation even though Max holds the gun.

sections.md:
Max explains (or allows it to be understood) that he got into the locked room easily — with a **passkey** or similar trick. Ausable then makes a grumbling complaint that sounds completely harmless. He says that this is the **second time** in a month that somebody has got into his room — and that the earlier intruder came **through the balcony**. The balcony, he says, belongs to the next room and runs beneath his window. He adds that he had complained to the hotel management and that they had promised to block it off, but nothing had been done.

Read this moment carefully, because the whole story turns on it. Ausable is doing three things at once:

1. **Inventing a fact** — a balcony under the window.
2. **Making it believable** — by adding everyday details: an earlier intruder, complaints to the management, a broken promise. Lies sound true when they are wrapped in ordinary grumbling.
3. **Making it sound unimportant** — he does not say 'You could escape this way'. He says it as an irritated aside, so Max does not suspect a trap.

Max glances towards the window. He says nothing, but the idea has entered his mind. Neither Fowler nor the reader yet knows that the balcony is pure fiction. This is the writer's cleverest move: like Max, *we* believe Ausable.

check.q: Why did Ausable mention the balcony in an irritated, offhand way?
options: He really wanted the management to fix it
So that Max would believe in it without suspecting a trap
check.why: By presenting the invented balcony as a boring complaint, Ausable made Max accept it as fact and remember it as a possible escape route.

sections.h: Scene 4 — The knock at the door
sections.md:
Max is unmoved by the talk of balconies; he simply wants the report. He sits waiting, gun ready. Then there is a sharp **knock at the door**.

Ausable stays calm and explains, as if it were the most natural thing, that this must be the **police**. He says that, since the paper was so important, he had asked for protection, and the police had promised to call and check on him.

Now the pressure shifts completely. A moment ago Max was in command. Now he is the one in danger: if the police find an armed foreign agent in the room, he will be arrested. He becomes nervous and threatening. He tells Ausable to get rid of the visitors, and warns that if anyone tries to come in he will shoot.

Then, under pressure, Max makes the decision Ausable has been steering him towards. He announces that he will **hide on the balcony** outside the window until the police have gone — and that Ausable had better send them away, or else. Keeping the pistol pointed, he backs to the window, swings a leg over the sill, steps out, and lets himself drop to the balcony he believes lies just below.

There is a **scream** — a short, fading cry that dies away. The balcony was never there. Max has fallen from the sixth floor.

check.q: What made Max decide to go out of the window?
options: He saw the missile report outside
He feared arrest by the 'police' and believed there was a balcony to hide on
check.why: Max believed both lies: that the police were at the door and that a balcony lay below the window — so he chose to hide there.

sections.h: Scene 5 — The waiter and the truth
sections.md:
The door opens. It is not the police at all. It is a **waiter** carrying a tray with a bottle and two glasses — the drinks Ausable had ordered earlier in the evening. Ausable calmly tells him to put the tray on the table and leave.

Fowler, shaken, stammers out his questions. What about the police? Ausable answers that **there were no police**: the knock was only the waiter he had been expecting. And the balcony? Ausable admits that **there is no balcony**. He had made it up on the spot.

The story ends quietly and swiftly, with no gloating speech. Ausable does not boast. The ending's very calmness is what makes it chilling and memorable.

**Did Ausable plan everything?** Not in advance. He knew two facts: there was no balcony, and a waiter would soon knock. In the moments after finding Max, he connected these facts into a plan. That is what makes him brilliant — not preparation but **instant, creative thinking**.

head: Step
What Ausable says or does
The truth
rows: Says intruders have come through 'the balcony'
Adds that management promised to block it
Lets Max choose to hide 'on the balcony'
Max falls from the sixth floor
fig.caption: Ausable's web of truth and invention.

check.q: Who actually knocked at the door?
options: A waiter bringing the drinks Ausable had ordered
check.why: Ausable had ordered drinks earlier; he pretended the knock was the police to frighten Max into using the imaginary balcony.

sections.h: How the plot is built: suspense, irony and the twist
sections.md:
Map the story on a simple plot curve:

| Stage | Event |
|---|---|
| Exposition | Fowler and Ausable climb to the room; Fowler is disappointed |
| Rising action | Max with a pistol; the balcony 'complaint' |
| Climax | The knock; Max goes out of the window |
| Falling action | The scream; the waiter enters |
| Resolution | Ausable reveals: no police, no balcony |

**Suspense** is created by short scenes, a threat (the pistol), a ticking clock (the paper will arrive; someone will knock) and a confident villain.

**Irony** runs through the story. Fowler wanted excitement from a glamorous spy; he gets it from the least glamorous man imaginable. Max, who looked like the 'real' spy, is the one who is fooled. This is **situational irony** — the outcome is the opposite of what we expect.

**Foreshadowing:** the 'sixth floor' and Ausable's casual mention of having ordered things earlier prepare the ending. On a second reading, you notice every clue.

**The twist** works because it is *fair*: nothing in the story contradicts it, and it explains everything. A good twist should make the reader say, 'Of course!' rather than 'That's impossible!'

sections.md:
**Ausable** — The hero. Physically unimpressive: fat, slow, sloppy, with an American accent. Mentally extraordinary: calm under pressure, observant, quick-witted, imaginative and an expert in human psychology. He understands that a frightened man grabs the first escape route offered. He wins without violence of his own and without boasting. He is the opposite of the film-spy stereotype — and that is the point.

**Fowler** — A young writer, romantic and naive. He stands in for the reader: he has the same expectations we do, and he is just as surprised by the ending. Through his eyes we first underestimate Ausable, and through his shock we feel the twist.

**Max** — The rival agent. Slim, smart, armed and confident; he looks like the 'real thing'. His weaknesses are **over-confidence** and **panic under pressure**. He never questions Ausable's story, never checks the window, and never asks why a careful spy would mention a weak point in his own room.

**The waiter** — A minor character, but crucial: his ordinary errand becomes the trigger for the climax.

| Trait | Ausable | Max |
|---|---|---|
| Appearance | Fat, unglamorous | Slim, stylish |
| Weapon | Wit | Pistol |
| Under pressure | Calm | Panics |
| Result | Wins | Falls |

check.q: Which weakness of Max did Ausable exploit?
options: His fear of being caught and his readiness to believe a convenient escape
check.why: Max panicked at the thought of police and trusted the 'balcony' without checking — exactly the reactions Ausable counted on.

sections.md:
1. **Appearances are deceptive.** The man who looks least like a spy is the most effective one; the one who looks most like a spy is beaten.
2. **Intelligence over force.** A gun loses to an idea. Ausable shows that the mind is the strongest weapon.
3. **Presence of mind.** In a crisis, calm thinking creates options that panic destroys. This is a life skill, not just a spy skill — useful in exams, in emergencies and in arguments.
4. **Romance versus reality.** Fowler's dream of glamorous espionage is replaced by a reality that is quieter but far more impressive.
5. **The power of a story.** Ausable defeats Max with a story. A believable lie, told with the right details at the right moment, changes someone's actions.

**A value-based note:** Ausable uses deception against an armed criminal threatening him. In ordinary life, honesty matters; the lesson to take is *calm, clever thinking*, not lying.

**Did you know?** Detective and spy fiction often uses the 'least likely hero' — think of Agatha Christie's small, fussy Hercule Poirot or G.K. Chesterton's humble Father Brown. Readers love seeing the underestimated person win.
keyTerms: situational irony — when the outcome is the opposite of what was expected
foreshadowing — hints that prepare for later events
stereotype — a fixed, oversimplified idea of what a type of person is like

sections.md:
**Vocabulary from the story's world**
- *espionage* — spying
- *passkey* — a key that opens several locks
- *sill* — the ledge at the bottom of a window
- *musty* — smelling stale and damp
- *stout / plump* — fat
- *snarl* — speak angrily, like an animal baring teeth
- *gloat* — take smug pleasure in someone's failure
- *rendezvous* — a secret meeting

**Grammar in action — direct and reported speech.** The story is told largely through dialogue, which keeps it quick like a play. Practise converting:
- Direct: Ausable said, "There is no balcony." → Reported: Ausable said that there was no balcony.
- Direct: Max said, "I will wait on the balcony." → Reported: Max said that he would wait on the balcony.
- Direct: Fowler asked, "Where are the police?" → Reported: Fowler asked where the police were.

**Drama activity.** Turn the story into a short play with four roles (Ausable, Fowler, Max, the waiter). Notice how easily it fits: one room, one evening, few characters — the classic 'one-act' format.

check.q: Change to reported speech: Max said, "I will shoot if anyone enters."
options: Max said that he will shoot if anyone enters.
Max said that he would shoot if anyone entered.
Max said that I would shoot if anyone entered.
Max says he shot if anyone entered.
check.why: With a past reporting verb, 'will' becomes 'would' and 'enters' becomes 'entered'; 'I' becomes 'he'.

sections.md:
**Q. How was Ausable different from other secret agents?** He did not fit the popular image. He was fat, untidy, lived in a dull hotel room and spoke with an American accent. Yet he was sharp, calm and quick-witted, and defeated an armed rival purely by intelligence.

**Q. Who was Max? How did he get in?** A rival secret agent who wanted the missile report; he entered the locked room using a passkey and waited with a pistol.

**Q. Why did Ausable talk about the balcony?** To plant in Max's mind the idea of an escape route, so that when a threat arrived Max would use it. The details about earlier intruders and management's broken promise made it believable.

**Q. 'Ausable did not fit Fowler's picture of a secret agent.' What was Fowler's picture?** Fowler imagined mystery, beautiful women, secret messages and gunfire — a glamorous, thrilling life.

**Q. Was Fowler's wish for excitement fulfilled?** Yes, but not as he expected: the excitement came through Ausable's quiet cleverness rather than glamour.

**Q. (Long answer) 'Presence of mind is a great asset.' Discuss with reference to the story.** Introduce the situation (armed rival, valuable paper). Show how Ausable stayed calm, invented the balcony, turned an ordinary knock into a threat, and let Max defeat himself. Conclude with how this skill helps in real life — staying calm in emergencies, exams and conflicts.

parts.md: During a power cut at a Shimla hotel, a schoolboy, Kabir, followed the old caretaker, Gupta-ji, to the basement generator room. A young man in a black jacket stepped out of the dark and demanded the keys to the hotel safe. Gupta-ji, slow and plump, sighed. 'Take them. But be careful — the back stairs flood when it rains; last week a guest slipped there. The front stairs have a guard tonight.'

Footsteps sounded above. 'The guard,' Gupta-ji whispered. The man bolted for the 'back stairs' door — straight into a storeroom with a self-latching lock, where he stayed until the police arrived. The footsteps had been Kabir's sister, bringing tea. 'There are no back stairs,' Gupta-ji told Kabir, sipping. Kabir grinned: 'Just like Ausable.' Brains, not bravado.

summary: Author: Robert Arthur (1909–1969), American writer of mystery and suspense.
Ausable is a fat, unglamorous secret agent living on the sixth floor of a French hotel.
Fowler, a young writer, expects a glamorous spy and is disappointed.
Ausable mentions an important paper about new missiles expected that night.
In the room they find Max, a rival agent, with a pistol, wanting the paper; he had used a passkey.
Ausable invents a balcony below his window through which an intruder had come before.
He adds believable details: complaints to management, a promise not kept.
A knock comes; Ausable claims it is the police he asked for.
Max decides to hide on the 'balcony', climbs out and drops — there is no balcony; he falls.
The knock was a waiter bringing the drinks Ausable had ordered.
Plot features: suspense, situational irony, foreshadowing, twist ending.
Themes: appearances deceive; intelligence over force; presence of mind.
Fowler represents the reader; Max represents over-confidence.

take smug pleasure in someone's failure

rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-question-of-t.title: A Question of Trust — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-question-of-t.subtitle: A respectable burglar, a charming lady in red, and the oldest lesson in the book: there is no honour among thieves

sections.h: A hook: can a thief be cheated?
sections.md:
Imagine a man so careful that he robs only **one safe a year**, plans each job for weeks, never hurts anyone, and spends his loot on **rare books**. He thinks he has thought of everything. Then a smiling young woman in a red dress walks into the room he is robbing — and within ten minutes she has turned him into her unpaid servant, and later into a prisoner.

*A Question of Trust* is by **Victor Canning** (1911–1986), a popular British writer of thrillers and short stories. Since Canning died after 1965 his work is still in copyright, so this companion **retells** the story scene by scene in our own words and explains it; read the original text in *Footprints without Feet* (free official PDF linked at the end).

The title is ironic. Horace Danby is a thief who expects people to **trust** him as a respectable citizen — and he himself trusts a stranger far too easily. The story asks: what happens when a dishonest man meets someone more dishonest than he is?
keyTerms: irony — a contrast between what is expected and what actually happens
burglar — a person who breaks into buildings to steal
no honour among thieves — dishonest people cannot rely on one another

check.q: Why did Horace Danby rob a safe every year?
options: To buy the rare, expensive books he loved
To take revenge on the rich
check.why: His one passion was collecting rare books, and he stole once a year to afford them.

sections.md:
On the chosen afternoon, with the servants away, Horace slips through the garden to the back of the house. He takes the key from its hiding place and enters quietly.

The dog **Sammy** comes up to him — but Horace has learnt its name. He speaks to it gently, calling 'Sammy', and the dog, recognising its name, wags its tail and goes back to its basket. Horace's research has paid off.

He goes into the drawing room, takes down the painting and finds the safe. He puts on his gloves and begins to work. Everything is going exactly to plan — except that the flowers in the house are making his nose itch and he wants to sneeze.

The writer slows down the action here, giving us Horace's confidence and his little discomforts, so that we feel as safe as he does — and are just as unprepared for what happens next.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#f7fafc'/><rect x='40' y='60' width='520' height='210' fill='#fefcbf' stroke='#744210' stroke-width='4'/><rect x='240' y='90' width='120' height='100' fill='#718096' stroke='#2d3748' stroke-width='4'/><circle cx='300' cy='140' r='22' fill='#a0aec0' stroke='#2d3748' stroke-width='3'/><line x1='300' y1='140' x2='300' y2='122' stroke='#2d3748' stroke-width='4'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='rotate' values='0 300 140;120 300 140;-60 300 140;0 300 140' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line><text x='300' y='215' text-anchor='middle' font-size='14' fill='#2d3748'>the safe (behind a painting)</text><g transform='translate(110 250)'><rect x='-12' y='-70' width='24' height='70' fill='#2d3748'/><circle cy='-82' r='14' fill='#f6e0c8'/><text y='18' text-anchor='middle' font-size='13'>Horace</text></g><g transform='translate(480 250)'><path d='M-22 0 L0 -75 L22 0z' fill='#e53e3e'><animate attributeName='opacity' values='0;1;1' dur='3s' fill='freeze'/></path><circle cy='-86' r='13' fill='#f6e0c8'/><text y='18' text-anchor='middle' font-size='13'>lady in red</text></g><text x='60' y='40' font-size='16' fill='#744210'>Shotover Grange — drawing room</text></svg>

sections.md:
Suddenly a voice speaks behind him. Horace turns to see a **young and pretty woman in a red dress** standing in the doorway, smiling. She does not scream or call the police. She speaks calmly, even with amusement.

She tells him — or lets him believe — that she is the **lady of the house**. She says she had come back early, that she could easily ring the police, and that a man like him would go to prison. Horace, caught red-handed, is frightened and ashamed.

Then she offers him a way out. She explains that she wants her **jewels** from the safe because she is going to a party — but she has **forgotten the combination**, and her husband is away. If Horace opens the safe for her, she will not report him.

Horace is relieved. He thinks this is a lucky escape. But the safe is tricky, and to do the job well he **takes off his gloves**. He opens the safe, and the lady in red takes out the jewels, thanks him, and sends him off. To cap it all, she even offers him something to smoke and is charming throughout.

Horace walks away, thinking he has been fortunate. He has not noticed the obvious questions: Why would the owner not call a locksmith? Why did she show no fear of a burglar? Why so calm?

check.q: Why did Horace take off his gloves?
options: His hands were sweating from fear
He wanted to impress the lady
To work the difficult safe properly for the lady
check.why: Believing he was helping the owner and no longer in danger, he removed his gloves to open the safe — leaving fingerprints.

sections.h: Scene 4 — Arrested, and nobody believes him
sections.md:
A few days later Horace is **arrested** for stealing the jewels of Shotover Grange. His **fingerprints** are all over the safe and the room, because he had worked without gloves.

At the trial he tells the truth: that a young woman in red, the lady of the house, had asked him to open the safe. But the real lady of the house is **an older woman**, and she had been away. Nobody else saw the woman in red. Horace's story sounds like the excuse any burglar would make, and **no one believes him**.

The truth dawns on Horace: the woman was **a thief herself**, perhaps one who had been watching the house too. She had used him — a skilled safe-breaker — to do her work, and left him to take the blame. She was *cleverer* at crime than he was.

Horace is sent to **prison**. There, he works as an assistant in the prison **library**. With bitter irony, he still thinks of the woman in red and wonders who she was. The story ends with him sure that he will never trust a charming woman again — the man who lived by deception has been undone by a deception he trusted.

check.q: Why did nobody believe Horace's story?
options: The real lady of the house was older and had been away, and no one else had seen the woman in red
He changed his story many times
check.why: The description did not match the real owner and there was no witness — so his account seemed like a burglar's invention.

sections.h: How the plot works: irony and the trap
sections.md:
| Stage | Event |
|---|---|
| Exposition | Horace's double life; the plan for Shotover Grange |
| Rising action | Entry; Sammy quieted; working on the safe |
| Climax | The lady in red catches him |
| Falling action | He opens the safe without gloves; she takes the jewels |
| Resolution | Arrest, trial, prison library |

**The irony of the title.** Horace expects to be trusted (his public image is of an honest man) and trusts the woman in red. He is betrayed by trust. A thief, who exploits other people's trust, falls into a trap of misplaced trust.

**Situational irony.** The careful planner, who thought of the dog, the servants and the key, did not think of another criminal. All his precautions — gloves especially — are undone by a simple appeal.

**Character irony.** The woman's charm hides her ruthlessness; Horace's respectability hides his crimes. Both wear masks.

**The 'locked-room' detail.** Horace fails to ask the obvious questions. The writer shows how fear and relief cloud judgement: a frightened person grabs any lifeline.

right.title: What he missed
points: Did not question why the 'owner' couldn't call a locksmith

sections.md:
**Horace Danby**
- Respectable on the surface: a good locksmith, quiet bachelor, booklover.
- Secretly a thief, once a year, for fifteen years — methodical and patient.
- Gentle (makes friends with the dog, harms no one), but morally confused: he treats theft as harmless.
- Suffers from hay fever — a small human weakness that the writer uses to make him seem ordinary.
- His fatal flaws: **over-confidence** and **gullibility**. He is so relieved to escape that he trusts a stranger without question.

**The lady in red**
- Young, charming, poised and very clever.
- A professional thief who uses charm instead of tools.
- Quick to read people: she sees Horace's fear and gives him an easy escape — on her terms.
- Morally she is worse than Horace: she not only steals but lets an innocent-of-this-crime man take the blame.

**Sammy** — the dog, a small proof of Horace's planning.

**Comparison:** Horace is a craftsman of crime; the woman is a psychologist of crime. In a contest between skill and psychology, psychology wins.

check.q: Which word best describes the lady in red?
check.why: She tricked a skilled burglar into opening the safe and taking the blame — clever and deceitful, i.e. cunning.

sections.md:
1. **Crime does not pay.** However careful the criminal, wrongdoing eventually catches up. Horace's fifteen years of success end in prison.
2. **There is no honour among thieves.** One criminal cannot trust another.
3. **Appearances deceive.** The woman looks like a lady; Horace looks like a respectable citizen. Neither is what they seem.
4. **Trust and judgement.** Trust is valuable, but blind trust in strangers — especially when you are under pressure — is dangerous.
5. **Ends do not justify means.** Horace's love of beautiful books is a fine passion, but stealing to pay for it is wrong. A good goal does not excuse a bad method.

**Did you know?** Stories of a 'cheater cheated' are very old. Indian folk tales — the Panchatantra's crafty jackal outwitted by a cleverer animal, or Tenali Raman catching thieves at their own game — use the same pattern, because readers enjoy seeing pride brought low.

**Words to know:** *respectable* (seen as decent and honest), *burglar*, *combination* (the number code of a safe), *hay fever* (allergy to pollen causing sneezing), *gullible* (easily deceived), *drawing room* (sitting room in a large house), *red-handed* (in the very act of a crime).

**Idioms in the story's spirit:**
- *caught red-handed* — caught in the act
- *to fall into a trap*
- *to take someone for a ride* — to cheat them
- *to pay the price*

**Grammar practice (reported speech):**
- She said, "I have forgotten the combination." → She said that she had forgotten the combination.
- Horace asked, "Will you call the police?" → Horace asked whether she would call the police.
- She said to him, "Open the safe." → She told him to open the safe.

check.q: 'Caught red-handed' means:
options: Caught with paint on one's hands
Caught in the act of doing wrong
Caught by a woman in red
check.why: The idiom means discovered in the very act of a crime or misdeed.

sections.md:
**Q. Who was Horace Danby? Was he a typical thief?** A respectable, unmarried locksmith of about fifty who robbed one safe a year to buy rare books. He was not typical: he was polite, planned carefully, harmed no one and stole only once a year.

**Q. How did he prepare for the Shotover Grange robbery?** He studied the house for two weeks, learnt the servants' timings, the dog's name, where the key and safe were, and carried gloves and tools.

**Q. How did the lady in red trick him?** By posing as the owner, threatening police, then offering to let him go if he opened the safe for her 'forgotten' jewels. He removed his gloves, opened the safe, and she took the jewels.

**Q. Why is the story called 'A Question of Trust'?** Horace, who abused others' trust, trusted a stranger and was betrayed; the title points to the irony of trust between dishonest people.

**Q. (Long answer) 'Horace Danby was good and respectable — but not completely honest.' Discuss.** Describe his public image and kindness; then his annual thefts and self-justification; conclude that honesty cannot be part-time and that his fall teaches that crime ultimately does not pay.

parts.md: At New Delhi station, Arjun, a smart pickpocket who boasted he had never been caught, lifted a wallet from a traveller and slipped into the crowd. A pleasant young man in a crisp shirt fell into step beside him. 'Police checking bags at gate four,' he whispered. 'Give me the wallet; I'm a porter here, they never search us. Meet me at the tea stall.'

Arjun handed it over gratefully. He waited at the tea stall for an hour. The 'porter' never came. Later, CCTV caught Arjun lifting the wallet — but not the second man. Sitting in the station police room, Arjun finally understood the oldest lesson of all: a cheat cannot trust a cheat.

summary: Author: Victor Canning (1911–1986), British thriller writer.
Horace Danby, about fifty, is a respectable, unmarried locksmith.
Secretly he robs one safe a year to buy rare books; never caught in fifteen years.
He plans to rob Shotover Grange after studying it for two weeks.
He knows the servants' cinema afternoon, the dog Sammy's name, the hidden key and safe.
He suffers from hay fever — the flowers trouble him.
A young woman in red catches him, pretending to be the lady of the house.
She asks him to open the safe for her 'forgotten' jewels instead of calling police.
He takes off his gloves, opens the safe; she takes the jewels.
He is arrested on fingerprint evidence; no one believes his story.
The real owner is older; the woman in red was a cleverer thief.
Horace ends up as a prison library assistant.
Themes: crime does not pay; no honour among thieves; misplaced trust; appearances deceive.

rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-the-necklace.title: The Necklace — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-the-necklace.subtitle: One borrowed necklace, one glittering night, and ten years of hard labour for a mistake that never needed to happen

sections.h: A hook: what would you give for one perfect evening?
sections.md:
Suppose you could look like a film star for one night — admired, envied, the centre of every eye. Would you pay for it with ten years of your life? Matilda Loisel never meant to make that bargain. But one borrowed necklace, one ball and one moment of pride locked her into exactly that.

*The Necklace* is by the French master of the short story **Guy de Maupassant** (1850–1893). He wrote around three hundred short stories, famous for sharp observation of ordinary people, economy of words and **surprise endings**. The story first appeared in French as *La Parure* in 1884. Maupassant's work is in the public domain, but the version in your NCERT book is an **adapted English translation**, and we cannot be certain of its exact wording; so this companion gives a **complete scene-by-scene retelling** in our own words, explanation of every part, and exam work. Read the textbook version alongside (free PDF linked at the end).

**Setting:** Paris in the late 19th century, a society where class and appearance mattered enormously. A clerk's wife could not easily mix with the rich — except at an official ball.
keyTerms: short story — brief fiction focused on a single incident and a few characters
surprise ending — a final twist that changes the meaning of the whole story
vanity — excessive pride in one's appearance

sections.md:
**Matilda** is pretty and charming, but she has been born into a family of clerks. With no dowry and no prospects, she marries **Monsieur Loisel**, a modest clerk in the **Ministry of Education** (Board of Education in some versions).

She dresses plainly because she cannot afford anything else, but she is **unhappy all the time**. She feels she was born for luxury: she dreams of silent halls with oriental hangings, tall bronze lamps, footmen in short breeches, elegant salons with silk, delicate dinners on fine dishes, and admiring gentlemen. Her own small apartment, with its worn chairs and shabby walls, torments her. Even her maid's simple work reminds her of what she lacks.

She has a rich friend from convent school, **Madame Forestier**, but she stops visiting her because every visit leaves her miserable with envy.

Matilda has no fine dresses and no jewels — *nothing* — and she loves only those things. Her husband, by contrast, is simple and content: when a stew is served he says happily that there is nothing better.

**Understanding Matilda:** her problem is not poverty so much as **dissatisfaction**. She measures her life against a dream and finds it always falling short. This is the seed of her tragedy.

check.q: Why was Matilda always unhappy?
options: She felt she deserved a life of luxury that she did not have
check.why: Matilda believed she was born for elegance and riches, so her modest life with a clerk made her constantly discontented.

sections.h: Part 2 — The invitation and the dress
sections.md:
One evening Loisel comes home proudly with a large envelope. It is an **invitation from the Minister of Education** and his wife to a ball (an official reception) at the ministry. He has gone to great trouble to get it, expecting his wife to be delighted.

Instead, Matilda throws it on the table and bursts into tears. 'What do you want me to do with this?' she asks in effect. She has **nothing to wear**; she cannot go.

Loisel is upset. He asks how much a suitable dress would cost. Matilda calculates carefully — a sum that a careful clerk would not refuse out of shock — and names **four hundred francs**. Loisel turns a little pale: he had saved exactly that sum to buy a **gun** for hunting trips with friends the next summer. But he agrees, and gives her the money. This is his first sacrifice.

As the day of the ball draws near, Matilda again seems sad and anxious. Her dress is ready, but she has **no jewels**, not even a single stone. She would look poverty-stricken, she says. Loisel suggests natural flowers — fashionable and cheap. She refuses. Then he has an idea: borrow jewels from her friend **Madame Forestier**.

check.q: What sacrifice did Loisel make for the dress?
options: He gave up the 400 francs he had saved to buy a gun
check.why: Loisel had saved 400 francs for a gun for summer hunting and gave it to Matilda for the dress instead.

sections.md:
The next day Matilda visits Madame Forestier and explains her trouble. Her friend, kindly, brings out a large jewel box and tells her to choose.

Matilda looks at bracelets, a pearl necklace, a Venetian cross of gold and jewels. She tries them on before the mirror, hesitating, unable to give them up — but she keeps asking whether there is anything else.

Then she finds, in a black satin box, a superb **necklace of diamonds** (so it appears). Her heart beats with desire. Her hands tremble as she fastens it around her neck, and she stands in ecstasy before her reflection. She asks anxiously whether she may borrow *only that*. Madame Forestier says, of course.

Matilda hugs her friend warmly and hurries away with her treasure.

**Notice:** Matilda never asks the necklace's value, and Madame Forestier never mentions it. This silence is the hinge of the entire plot.

sections.h: Part 4 — The ball and the loss
sections.md:
On the night of the ball Matilda is a **great success**. She is the prettiest woman there — elegant, graceful, smiling, wild with joy. All the men look at her, ask her name and want to be introduced. Even the Minister notices her. She dances with pleasure, intoxicated by admiration, forgetting everything in a cloud of happiness. Her husband, meanwhile, has been half-asleep since midnight in a small room with three other gentlemen whose wives were also enjoying themselves.

At about **four in the morning** they leave. Loisel throws over her shoulders the modest wraps of everyday life, whose poverty clashes with the ball dress. She hurries away so that the rich ladies wrapped in furs will not see her. They cannot find a cab at first and walk down towards the Seine, shivering, until they find an old night cab.

At home, before the mirror, Matilda takes off her wraps to see herself once more in her glory — and suddenly cries out. **The necklace is gone.**

Loisel, already half undressed, is horrified. They search the folds of the dress, the cloak, the pockets — everywhere. Nothing. They did not note the cab's number. Loisel goes back over the whole route they had walked; then to the police, to the cab offices, and puts advertisements in the newspapers offering a reward. Nothing.

After a week they have lost all hope. Loisel, aged five years in that week, says they must replace the necklace.

check.q: When did Matilda discover the necklace was missing?
options: At home, in front of the mirror
The next week at Madame Forestier's
check.why: She noticed the loss at home when she took off her wraps to admire herself once more in the mirror.

sections.h: Part 5 — Replacing it: the great debt
sections.md:
To buy time, Matilda writes to Madame Forestier (at Loisel's suggestion) saying that the clasp is broken and is being repaired.

The Loisels take the empty box to the jeweller whose name is inside. He did not sell that necklace, he says; he had only supplied the case. They go from jeweller to jeweller, searching for a necklace like it, sick with anxiety. At last, in a shop at the **Palais-Royal**, they find a string of diamonds that seems exactly like it. Its price is **forty thousand francs**; the jeweller will let them have it for **thirty-six thousand**.

Loisel has **eighteen thousand francs** left to him by his father. He **borrows the rest** — a thousand from one, five hundred from another, a few louis here and there. He signs notes, makes ruinous promises, deals with money-lenders of every kind. He compromises the rest of his life, risking his signature without knowing whether he can honour it.

They buy the necklace and Matilda returns it. Madame Forestier, a little cold, says she should have returned it sooner, as she might have needed it. She **does not open the case**. (Matilda had feared she would notice the substitution and think her a thief.)

| Item | Francs |
|---|---|
| Price asked | 40,000 |
| Price paid | 36,000 |
| Loisel's inheritance | 18,000 |
| Borrowed | 18,000 |

check.q: How much did the Loisels pay for the replacement necklace?
check.why: The jeweller asked 40,000 francs but sold it for 36,000; half came from Loisel's inheritance and half was borrowed.

sections.md:
Now Matilda learns the horrible life of the poor. She plays her part heroically. The terrible debt must be paid, and she will pay it.

- They **dismiss the maid** and move to a small **attic** under the roof.
- Matilda does the heavy housework herself: she washes dishes, wearing out her pink nails on greasy pots; she washes dirty linen, shirts and cloths and hangs them to dry; she carries the rubbish down and the water up every morning, stopping on each landing to breathe.
- Dressed like a woman of the people, she goes to the grocer, butcher and fruiterer with a basket, **bargaining** to save every sou.
- Each month some notes are paid off and others renewed to gain time.
- Loisel works in the evenings, keeping a merchant's accounts, and at night often copies manuscripts at five sous a page.

This life lasts **ten years**. At the end, they have repaid everything — with the money-lenders' interest and compound interest too.

Matilda now looks **old**. She has become a strong, hard, rough woman of a poor household, with uncombed hair, skirts askew and red hands, talking loudly and washing floors with large pails of water. Sometimes, when her husband is at the office, she sits by the window and thinks of that evening long ago, at the ball, where she had been so beautiful and admired. What would have happened if she had not lost the necklace? Who knows? How strange life is — how little is needed to ruin us or to save us!

One Sunday, walking in the **Champs-Élysées** to refresh herself after the week's work, Matilda sees a woman walking with a child. It is **Madame Forestier**, still young, still beautiful, still charming.

Matilda is moved. Should she speak to her? Yes — now that the debt is paid, she will tell her everything. She goes up and greets her. Madame Forestier does not recognise her and is surprised to be addressed so familiarly by this woman of the people. When Matilda names herself, her friend cries out in astonishment at how changed she is.

Matilda explains that she has had hard days since she last saw her, and miseries enough — all because of her. She tells the whole story: the lost necklace, the identical one bought to replace it, the ten years of paying for it. She smiles with proud and simple joy that it is over.

Madame Forestier stops, deeply moved, and takes both her hands. Her reply is the story's famous final blow: her necklace had been **imitation** — **paste**, false diamonds — worth **at most five hundred francs**.

Ten years of toil had been spent to replace something nearly worthless.

sections.md:
**Matilda Loisel** — pretty, charming, dreamy and deeply discontented; vain and materialistic at first, living for appearances. Her fatal flaws are **vanity**, **pride** and a failure to be honest when the necklace is lost. Yet she also shows **courage and integrity**: she shoulders the debt heroically and pays every sou. Her character changes from a self-pitying dreamer to a hardened, honest working woman — a dynamic character.

**Monsieur Loisel** — simple, content, loving and self-sacrificing. He gives up his gun money, searches all night, gives his inheritance, borrows, and works night after night. He is the story's quiet hero, though he too shares the mistake of not telling the truth.

**Madame Forestier** — rich, generous (she lends freely) but slightly cold when the necklace is returned late. She never mentions that the jewels are fake — perhaps it never occurred to her that anyone would think them real.

| Matilda before | Matilda after |
|---|---|
| Delicate, pretty | Rough, aged |
| Dreams of luxury | Knows real hardship |
| Vain, discontented | Hardworking, honest |
| Has a maid | Does all the work herself |

1. **Vanity and pride lead to downfall.** Matilda's wish to appear rich for one evening costs her ten years.
2. **Appearance versus reality.** The necklace looks priceless but is fake — exactly like the glittering world Matilda envied. Her own appearance also changes completely.
3. **Honesty is the best policy.** Had Matilda simply told her friend the truth, she would have learnt that the necklace was cheap. One lie (the 'broken clasp') led to a decade of suffering.
4. **Contentment.** Loisel is content with simple stew; Matilda is never content. Wanting what you do not have can destroy what you do have.
5. **Dignity of labour and responsibility.** In poverty, Matilda shows real strength and honour by repaying the debt.
6. **Chance and fate.** 'How little is needed to ruin us or to save us.'

**Irony:** Matilda's moment of triumph causes her ruin; she gives up her beauty to pay for an ornament meant to enhance it; the whole sacrifice was for a fake. This is a classic **surprise ending** — Maupassant's trademark.

**Did you know?** Maupassant was a protégé of the novelist Gustave Flaubert, who taught him to observe closely and choose exact words. *The Necklace* is among the most-taught short stories in the world.

check.q: Which single action could have prevented the Loisels' ten years of hardship?
options: Telling Madame Forestier the truth about the loss
Taking a cab with a number
check.why: If Matilda had confessed honestly, Madame Forestier would have told her the necklace was fake and worth very little.

sections.md:
**Q. What kind of person was Matilda?** Pretty and charming but discontented and vain; she dreamt of luxury and despised her modest life.

**Q. What was Loisel's reaction to Matilda's tears?** Distressed; he offered to buy her a dress, giving up the 400 francs saved for a gun, and suggested borrowing jewels.

**Q. Why did the Loisels not tell Madame Forestier about the loss?** Out of pride and fear of being thought thieves; they wrote that the clasp was being repaired to gain time.

**Q. How did the Loisels repay the debt?** By dismissing the maid, moving to an attic, Matilda doing all heavy housework and bargaining, Loisel doing extra accounts and copying work at night — for ten years.

**Q. (Long answer) 'The Necklace' shows how a small mistake can change one's life. Discuss.** Mention vanity, the loan, the loss, the lie, the debt, the transformation, and the irony of the fake necklace; conclude with the values of honesty and contentment.

**Q. (Long answer) Write a character sketch of M. Loisel.** Content, simple, loving, sacrificing; works tirelessly; shares the mistake of concealment.

parts.md: Riya borrowed her cousin's shiny new phone for her school farewell so the photos would look grand. After the party she found the back cracked. Too ashamed to say anything, she spent six months of pocket money and weekend tuition earnings on a replacement back panel and a new case, sneaking it in for repair before returning it.

When she finally confessed, her cousin laughed. 'That phone? It's a demo piece from my uncle's shop — it doesn't even make calls!' Riya groaned. 'Madame Forestier,' she muttered. 'Next time I'll just tell the truth on day one.'

rd-school-c10-english-b.grammar-1-tenses.title: Tenses, Modals, Subject–Verb Agreement and Determiners
rd-school-c10-english-b.grammar-1-tenses.subtitle: The four grammar engines behind every correct sentence — explained, tabled and drilled

sections.h: A hook: one word, four mistakes
sections.md:
Read this sentence from a real answer sheet: *"Each of the boys have went to a market yesterday and he can buys an apples."* Count the errors: **have** (should be *has*: concord), **went** after *have* (should be *gone*, or simply *went* without *have*: tense), **a market** (should be *the market*: determiner), **can buys** (should be *could buy*: modal), **an apples** (*an apple* or *some apples*: determiner). Five mistakes, four grammar systems.

This read covers all four systems in the Class 10 grammar syllabus: **tenses**, **modals**, **subject–verb agreement (concord)** and **determiners**. These are tested every year through gap-filling, editing, omission and sentence transformation. Master them and those questions become free marks.

**How to use this read:** study each table, try each check, then do the mixed practice at the end without looking back.
keyTerms: tense — the verb form that shows time (present, past, future) and aspect (simple, continuous, perfect)
modal — a helping verb showing ability, permission, possibility, obligation etc.
concord — agreement of the verb with its subject in number and person
determiner — a word before a noun that limits or identifies it (a, the, some, this, my…)

sections.md:
English has three **times** (present, past, future) and four **aspects** (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous) = 12 tense forms. Using the verb *play*:

| | Simple | Continuous | Perfect | Perfect continuous |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Present | play / plays | am/is/are playing | has/have played | has/have been playing |
| Past | played | was/were playing | had played | had been playing |
| Future | will play | will be playing | will have played | will have been playing |

**Uses you must know**
- **Simple present:** habits, universal truths, timetables. *The sun rises in the east. The train leaves at 6:10.*
- **Present continuous:** action now, or a fixed future plan. *She is writing. We are flying to Kochi tomorrow.*
- **Present perfect:** past action with present result, unfinished time, or with *just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for*. *I have lost my key. She has lived in Pune since 2019.*
- **Present perfect continuous:** action begun in the past and still going, stressing duration. *It has been raining for three hours.*
- **Simple past:** completed action at a stated past time. *We won the match yesterday.*
- **Past continuous:** action in progress at a past moment, often interrupted. *I was reading when the lights went out.*
- **Past perfect:** the earlier of two past actions. *The train had left before we reached.*
- **Future forms:** *will* for decisions/predictions; *be going to* for plans and evidence; simple present for timetables.

**Golden rule:** *never* use the present perfect with a definite past time word — say *I saw him yesterday*, not *I have seen him yesterday*.

check.q: Choose the correct form: 'She ___ in this school since 2021.'
check.why: 'Since 2021' marks an action that began in the past and continues now, which needs the present perfect continuous (or present perfect).

sections.h: Tense signals and sequence of tenses
sections.md:
**Signal words** are your shortcut in gap-filling:

| Signal | Usual tense |
|---|---|
| every day, usually, always, often | simple present |
| now, at present, look!, listen! | present continuous |
| just, already, yet, ever, never, so far | present perfect |
| since, for (with ongoing action) | present perfect (continuous) |
| yesterday, ago, last week, in 2010 | simple past |
| while, when (action in progress) | past continuous |
| before / after (two past actions) | past perfect for the earlier one |
| tomorrow, next year, soon | future |
| by the time (future) | future perfect |

**Sequence of tenses:** a past main verb is usually followed by a past form in the subordinate clause. *He said that he was tired. I knew that she had finished.* Exception: universal truths stay present — *The teacher said that water boils at 100 °C.*

**Conditionals (often tested):**
- Type 0: If you heat ice, it melts. (truth)
- Type 1: If it rains, we will stay in. (real future)
- Type 2: If I were rich, I would travel. (imaginary present)
- Type 3: If you had studied, you would have passed. (imaginary past)

**Did you know?** 'If I were' (not 'was') is the subjunctive — still the safe exam answer.

sections.md:
Modals (*can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to, need, dare, used to*) never take *-s*, *-ing* or *to* after them (except *ought to*, *used to*); they are followed by the **base verb**.

| Function | Modal | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Ability (present) | can | She can speak three languages. |
| Ability (past) | could | He could swim at six. |
| Permission (formal) | may | May I come in, sir? |
| Permission (informal) | can | Can I borrow your pen? |
| Possibility (more/less) | may / might | It may rain. It might snow in Manali. |
| Obligation / necessity | must, have to | You must wear a helmet. |
| Prohibition | must not | You must not cross on red. |
| No necessity | need not / don't have to | You need not hurry. |
| Advice / duty | should, ought to | You should exercise daily. We ought to respect elders. |
| Polite request | would, could | Would you please close the window? |
| Offer / suggestion | shall (with I/we) | Shall we start? |
| Determination / promise | will, shall | I will finish it tonight. |
| Past habit | used to, would | He used to walk to school. |
| Logical certainty | must | She has topped again; she must be very hardworking. |
| Courage | dare | How dare you! |

**Modal + perfect** for the past: *should have gone* (advice too late), *must have forgotten* (deduction), *could have won* (unused ability), *needn't have bought* (unnecessary action done).

check.q: 'You ___ have told me earlier; I could have helped.' Choose the best modal.
check.why: 'Should have' + past participle expresses advice or regret about something that was not done in the past.

sections.h: Modals in context — making the right choice
sections.md:
Exam gap-fills give you a short passage where the **context** decides the modal. Ask: Is it ability, permission, possibility, obligation or advice? Is it present or past?

**Worked mini-passage:**
> Doctors say that we ___ (1) drink at least eight glasses of water a day. In summer we ___ (2) drink even more, otherwise we ___ (3) fall ill. Children ___ (4) not drink water from open taps.

1. *should* — advice. 2. *must* / *should* — necessity/strong advice. 3. *may* / *might* / *can* — possibility. 4. *should* / *must* — prohibition/advice.

**Common errors:**
- ✘ *He can to swim.* ✔ *He can swim.*
- ✘ *She musts go.* ✔ *She must go.*
- ✘ *You must not to shout.* ✔ *You must not shout.*
- ✘ *I could went.* ✔ *I could go* / *I could have gone.*
- *Must not* (forbidden) ≠ *need not* (not necessary): *You must not smoke here.* vs *You need not bring lunch; it is provided.*

**Did you know?** *Shall* with *I/we* in questions is still the standard polite offer in Indian English and British English: 'Shall I carry your bag?'

**Basic rule:** a singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb. *The boy plays. The boys play.*

**The twelve rules that are tested:**
1. **Words between subject and verb do not change the subject.** *The box of chocolates **is** on the table. The quality of the mangoes **was** excellent.*
2. **And** joins two subjects → plural. *Ravi and Meena **are** friends.* But one idea/person → singular: *Bread and butter **is** my breakfast. The secretary and treasurer **has** arrived* (one person).
3. **Each, every, either, neither, everyone, somebody, nobody** → singular. *Each of the students **has** a book. Neither of them **is** ready.*
4. **Either…or / neither…nor / not only…but also** → verb agrees with the **nearer** subject. *Neither the teacher nor the students **were** present. Either the boys or Rina **is** coming.*
5. **As well as, along with, together with, with, besides** → verb agrees with the **first** subject. *The captain, along with his players, **was** honoured.*
6. **Collective nouns** (team, jury, family, committee): singular when acting as one unit, plural when members act individually. *The team **has** won. The jury **were** divided in their opinions.*
7. **Nouns plural in form but singular in meaning:** news, mathematics, physics, economics, measles → singular. *The news **is** good.*
8. **Always-plural nouns:** scissors, trousers, spectacles, cattle, police, people → plural. *The police **have** arrived.* (But *a pair of scissors **is**…*)
9. **Amounts of money, time, distance** as one unit → singular. *Five hundred rupees **is** too much. Ten kilometres **is** a long walk.*
10. **The number of** → singular; **a number of** → plural. *The number of cars **is** rising. A number of cars **are** parked outside.*
11. **Titles of books/films** → singular. *'Great Expectations' **is** a novel.*
12. **Relative pronoun** takes the number of its antecedent. *She is one of those girls who **sing** well.* But *She is the only one of the girls who **sings**.*

check.q: Choose the correct verb: 'Neither the principal nor the teachers ___ aware of the change.'
check.why: With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'teachers', which is plural.

sections.h: Concord — tricky cases and a drill
sections.md:
**More traps:**
- *There is / There are* agrees with the noun that follows: *There **is** a pen. There **are** two pens. There **is** a pen and two pencils* (nearer = *a pen*) — formal usage often prefers *are* for a combined list; follow your textbook examples and the nearer-noun rule.
- **Fractions and percentages** agree with the noun after *of*: *Half of the cake **is** eaten. Half of the students **are** absent. Forty per cent of the land **is** forest.*
- **One of + plural noun** → singular verb: *One of my friends **lives** in Goa.*
- **Many a** → singular: *Many a student **has** failed this test.*
- **Plural subject after a singular verb in questions:** *Where **are** my shoes?*

**Quick drill (answers in brackets):**
1. The list of items ___ on the desk. (is)
2. Mathematics ___ my favourite subject. (is)
3. The cattle ___ grazing. (are)
4. Every boy and girl ___ given a prize. (was)
5. The Prime Minister, with his ministers, ___ arrived. (has)
6. A number of students ___ absent. (were)
7. Twenty years ___ a long time. (is)
8. Either you or he ___ to blame. (is)
9. The committee ___ submitted its report. (has)
10. My spectacles ___ broken. (are)
