check.why: निदाघ (भीषण गर्मी) से सब लोग विकल हैं — यह मानव-जीवन के दुख और कष्टों का प्रतीक है।

sections.h: 📜 पूरा पाठ — अट नहीं रही है
sections.md:
> अट नहीं रही है
> आभा फागुन की तन
> सट नहीं रही है।
>
> कहीं साँस लेते हो,
> घर-घर भर देते हो,
> उड़ने को नभ में तुम
> पर-पर कर देते हो,
> आँख हटाता हूँ तो
> हट नहीं रही है।
>
> पत्तों से लदी डाल
> कहीं हरी, कहीं लाल,
> कहीं पड़ी है उर में
> मंद-गंध-पुष्प-माल,
> पाट-पाट शोभा-श्री
> पट नहीं रही है।

*(विराम-चिह्नों में पाठ्यपुस्तक से मामूली अंतर संभव है।)*

**'अट नहीं रही है आभा फागुन की तन सट नहीं रही है'** — फागुन की **आभा (शोभा, चमक)** इतनी अधिक है कि वह कहीं **समा (अट) नहीं** रही; वह शरीर (तन) में भी **सट (समा) नहीं** रही — प्रकृति के अंग-अंग से छलक रही है।

**'कहीं साँस लेते हो, घर-घर भर देते हो'** — हे फागुन! तुम जहाँ भी साँस लेते हो (तुम्हारी हवा जहाँ बहती है), वहाँ **घर-घर** को सुगंध से भर देते हो। (फागुन का **मानवीकरण** — वह साँस लेता है)

**'उड़ने को नभ में तुम पर-पर कर देते हो'** — तुम लोगों के मन को आकाश में उड़ने के लिए **पंख (पर)** लगा देते हो — मन उमंग से भर उठता है, कल्पना उड़ान भरने लगती है। ('पर-पर' — **पुनरुक्ति प्रकाश**; 'घर-घर', 'पर-पर' में तुक)

**'आँख हटाता हूँ तो हट नहीं रही है'** — फागुन का सौंदर्य इतना मनमोहक है कि कवि उससे आँख हटाना चाहे तो भी **आँख हट नहीं** पाती — दृष्टि वहीं बँध जाती है।

**'पत्तों से लदी डाल कहीं हरी, कहीं लाल'** — पेड़ों की डालियाँ नए पत्तों से **लदी** हैं — कहीं **हरे** पत्ते, कहीं **लाल** कोंपलें (नई पत्तियाँ लाल होती हैं)।

**'कहीं पड़ी है उर में मंद-गंध-पुष्प-माल'** — कहीं पेड़ों के **वक्ष (उर)** पर **धीमी सुगंध वाले फूलों की माला** पड़ी है — मानो प्रकृति ने फूलों का हार पहन लिया हो। (**मानवीकरण, उत्प्रेक्षा**)

**'पाट-पाट शोभा-श्री पट नहीं रही है'** — **जगह-जगह (पाट-पाट)** इतनी **शोभा और समृद्धि (शोभा-श्री)** बिखरी है कि वह कहीं **पट (समा)** नहीं रही — चारों ओर उमड़ रही है।

**केंद्रीय भाव:** फागुन की सर्वव्यापी, मादक सुंदरता — जो प्रकृति के कण-कण में और मनुष्य के मन में समाई है, फिर भी समा नहीं पाती।

check.q: 'आँख हटाता हूँ तो हट नहीं रही है' — इसका भाव है:
options: कवि की आँख में दर्द है
फागुन का सौंदर्य इतना मोहक है कि दृष्टि उससे हटती ही नहीं
कवि को कुछ दिखाई नहीं देता
check.why: कवि बताता है कि फागुन की शोभा इतनी आकर्षक है कि चाहकर भी आँखें उससे हट नहीं पातीं।

sections.md:
| पक्ष | उत्साह | अट नहीं रही है |
|---|---|---|
| विषय | बादल — क्रांति, नवजीवन | फागुन — वसंत का सौंदर्य |
| प्रकार | आह्वान गीत | प्रकृति-चित्रण, गीत |
| भाषा | तत्सम-प्रधान खड़ी बोली (*धाराधर, निदाघ, विद्युत-छबि, उन्मन*) | सरल, देशज-मिश्रित (*अट, सट, पट, पाट*) |
| ध्वनि | 'घेर घेर घोर गगन' — गर्जन जैसी कठोर ध्वनि | 'अट-सट-पट', 'घर-पर' — कोमल, मधुर तुक |
| रस | वीर/ओज गुण | शृंगार (प्रकृति), माधुर्य गुण |
| प्रमुख अलंकार | अनुप्रास, उपमा, मानवीकरण, पुनरुक्ति प्रकाश | मानवीकरण, पुनरुक्ति प्रकाश, अनुप्रास, उत्प्रेक्षा |

**अनुप्रास के उदाहरण:** 'घेर घेर घोर गगन' (घ), 'विकल विकल', 'मंद-गंध-पुष्प-माल'।
**मानवीकरण:** बादल को 'कवि' कहना; फागुन का साँस लेना; पेड़ों के उर पर फूलों की माला।
**उपमा:** 'बाल कल्पना के-से पाले'।

**निराला की विशेषता:** एक ही कवि दो बिलकुल अलग स्वर में लिखता है — एक में **ओज और विद्रोह**, दूसरे में **कोमलता और माधुर्य**। दोनों में **प्रकृति** मनुष्य के मन का दर्पण है।

**क्या आप जानते हैं?** निराला ने जब मुक्त छंद में लिखना शुरू किया (जैसे 'जूही की कली'), तब कई संपादकों ने उसे छापने से मना कर दिया था; आज वही मुक्त छंद आधुनिक हिंदी कविता की पहचान है।

check.q: 'घेर घेर घोर गगन' में कौन-सा अलंकार है?
check.why: 'घ' वर्ण की बार-बार आवृत्ति से अनुप्रास अलंकार बनता है, जो बादल की गर्जना का ध्वनि-चित्र भी देता है।

sections.md:
**प्र. कवि बादल से फुहार, रिमझिम या बरसने के स्थान पर 'गरजने' के लिए क्यों कहता है?** — गर्जना में क्रांति, ओज और परिवर्तन की शक्ति है; कवि समाज में नई चेतना और बदलाव चाहता है, केवल राहत नहीं।

**प्र. 'उत्साह' कविता में बादल किन-किन अर्थों की ओर संकेत करता है?** — (1) पीड़ित-प्यासे जन को राहत देने वाला; (2) नवजीवन, नई कल्पना देने वाला 'कवि'; (3) वज्र छिपाए क्रांतिकारी — पुरानी व्यवस्था को तोड़ने वाला।

**प्र. 'नवजीवन वाले' विशेषण से बादल का कौन-सा रूप सामने आता है?** — बादल वर्षा से सूखी धरती को नया जीवन देता है, वैसे ही निराश मनुष्यों में नई आशा भरता है।

**प्र. 'अट नहीं रही है' में फागुन की मादकता को कैसे प्रकट किया गया है?** — फागुन की आभा तन में नहीं समाती; उसकी साँस से घर-घर सुगंधित; मन में पंख लग जाते हैं; हरी-लाल डालियाँ, फूलों की माला; आँख हटाए नहीं हटती।

**प्र. फागुन में ऐसा क्या होता है जो बाकी ऋतुओं से भिन्न है?** — पेड़ नए पत्तों और फूलों से लद जाते हैं, हवा सुगंधित और मंद होती है, न अधिक सर्दी न गर्मी; होली का उल्लास; मन उमंग से भर जाता है।

**प्र. दोनों कविताओं में प्रकृति का कौन-सा रूप है?** — 'उत्साह' में उग्र, क्रांतिकारी; 'अट नहीं रही है' में कोमल, मोहक।

summary: कवि: सूर्यकांत त्रिपाठी 'निराला' (1899–1961), छायावाद के स्तंभ, मुक्त छंद के प्रवर्तक।
'उत्साह' एक आह्वान गीत है; बादल क्रांति, परिवर्तन और नवजीवन का प्रतीक है।
कवि बादल से 'गरजने' को कहता है — गर्जना जागरण और विद्रोह की हुंकार है।
बादल ललित, काले, घुँघराले, बालक की कल्पना जैसे; उसके उर में बिजली की छवि है।
बादल को 'कवि' और 'नवजीवन वाला' कहा गया; वज्र छिपाकर नई कविता भरने का आग्रह।
निदाघ (गर्मी) से विकल-उन्मन जन — दुखी मानवता का प्रतीक।
अज्ञात दिशा से आए बादल तपती धरती को शीतल करें — राहत और आशा।
'अट नहीं रही है' — फागुन की आभा इतनी है कि कहीं समा नहीं रही।
फागुन की साँस से घर-घर सुगंध; मन को उड़ने के पंख मिलते हैं; आँख हटाए नहीं हटती।
डालियाँ हरे-लाल पत्तों से लदीं, पेड़ों के उर पर मंद-गंध फूलों की माला।
'उत्साह' में ओज गुण और तत्सम भाषा; 'अट नहीं रही है' में माधुर्य और सरल तुकांत भाषा।
प्रमुख अलंकार: अनुप्रास, पुनरुक्ति प्रकाश, मानवीकरण, उपमा।
practice: कवि बादल से 'गरजने' के लिए क्यों कहता है?
'उत्साह' कविता का शीर्षक कहाँ तक सार्थक है?
कविता में बादल किन-किन अर्थों की ओर संकेत करता है?
'विद्युत-छबि उर में, कवि, नवजीवन वाले' — काव्य-सौंदर्य स्पष्ट कीजिए।
'तप्त धरा, जल से फिर शीतल कर दो' — भाव स्पष्ट कीजिए।
'अट नहीं रही है' कविता में फागुन की सुंदरता का वर्णन अपने शब्दों में कीजिए।
'उड़ने को नभ में तुम पर-पर कर देते हो' — आशय स्पष्ट कीजिए।
दोनों कविताओं की भाषा की तुलना कीजिए।
दोनों कविताओं से मानवीकरण और पुनरुक्ति प्रकाश के एक-एक उदाहरण लिखिए।
अपने क्षेत्र में वर्षा या वसंत के आगमन पर 120 शब्दों का अनुच्छेद लिखिए।

rd-school-c10-hindi-b.vyakaran.title: हिंदी व्याकरण — कक्षा 9–10 की संपूर्ण पुस्तिका
rd-school-c10-hindi-b.vyakaran.subtitle: वर्ण से वाक्य तक: संधि, समास, उपसर्ग-प्रत्यय, पदबंध, पद-परिचय, वाक्य भेद, वाच्य, अलंकार, रस और मुहावरे

sections.md:
जैसे किसी नए शहर में बिना नक्शे के भटकना आसान है, वैसे ही बिना व्याकरण के भाषा में भटकना। व्याकरण बताता है कि **वर्ण** मिलकर **शब्द** कैसे बनाते हैं, शब्द वाक्य में आकर **पद** कैसे बनते हैं, पद मिलकर **पदबंध** और **वाक्य** कैसे बनाते हैं, और वाक्य को सुंदर बनाने के लिए **अलंकार** और **रस** कैसे काम करते हैं।

इस पुस्तिका में कक्षा 9–10 के सभी व्याकरण विषय क्रम से हैं:
1. शब्द-निर्माण: **उपसर्ग, प्रत्यय, संधि, समास**
2. **पद और पदबंध**
3. **पद-परिचय**
4. **रचना के आधार पर वाक्य भेद** और **अर्थ के आधार पर वाक्य भेद**
5. **वाच्य**
6. **अलंकार**
7. **रस**
8. **मुहावरे और लोकोक्तियाँ**

हर भाग में परिभाषा, पहचान के सूत्र, उदाहरण-तालिका और एक जाँच-प्रश्न है।
keyTerms: वर्ण — भाषा की सबसे छोटी ध्वनि-इकाई
शब्द — वर्णों का सार्थक समूह
पद — वाक्य में प्रयुक्त शब्द
वाक्य — पदों का सार्थक, व्यवस्थित समूह

sections.md:
**उपसर्ग** — वे शब्दांश जो शब्द के **आरंभ** में जुड़कर उसका अर्थ बदल देते हैं।

| उपसर्ग | अर्थ | उदाहरण |
|---|---|---|
| अ / अन् | नहीं | अज्ञान, अनादर |
| प्र | आगे, अधिक | प्रगति, प्रबल |
| परा | उलटा | पराजय |
| सु | अच्छा | सुपुत्र, सुगम |
| दुर् / दुस् | बुरा | दुर्गुण, दुस्साहस |
| अभि | सामने | अभिमान, अभिनय |
| उप | निकट, छोटा | उपवन, उपमंत्री |
| वि | विशेष, अलग | विज्ञान, वियोग |
| सम् | अच्छी तरह | संयोग, संतोष |
| नि / निर् | रहित | निडर, निर्धन |
| बे, ला, ना (उर्दू) | बिना, नहीं | बेईमान, लापता, नापसंद |

**प्रत्यय** — वे शब्दांश जो शब्द के **अंत** में जुड़कर नया शब्द बनाते हैं।
- **कृत् प्रत्यय** (क्रिया/धातु से): पढ़ + **आई** = पढ़ाई; लिख + **आवट** = लिखावट; चल + **अन** = चलन; गा + **यक** = गायक।
- **तद्धित प्रत्यय** (संज्ञा, सर्वनाम, विशेषण से): मीठा + **आस** = मिठास; बुढ़ा + **पा** = बुढ़ापा; समाज + **इक** = सामाजिक; मानव + **ता** = मानवता; सुंदर + **ता** = सुंदरता; दुकान + **दार** = दुकानदार।

**उदाहरण (दोनों साथ):** **अ** + सफल + **ता** = असफलता; **सु** + गंध + **इत** = सुगंधित।

check.q: 'मिठास' शब्द में प्रत्यय है —
check.why: मीठा + आस = मिठास; 'आस' तद्धित प्रत्यय है।

sections.md:
दो वर्णों के मेल से होने वाले विकार को **संधि** कहते हैं। संधि तीन प्रकार की है।

**(क) स्वर संधि** (स्वर + स्वर)
| भेद | नियम | उदाहरण |
|---|---|---|
| दीर्घ | अ/आ + अ/आ = आ; इ/ई + इ/ई = ई; उ/ऊ + उ/ऊ = ऊ | विद्या + आलय = विद्यालय; रवि + इंद्र = रवींद्र; भानु + उदय = भानूदय |
| गुण | अ/आ + इ/ई = ए; अ/आ + उ/ऊ = ओ; अ/आ + ऋ = अर् | देव + इंद्र = देवेंद्र; महा + उत्सव = महोत्सव; महा + ऋषि = महर्षि |
| वृद्धि | अ/आ + ए/ऐ = ऐ; अ/आ + ओ/औ = औ | सदा + एव = सदैव; वन + औषधि = वनौषधि |
| यण् | इ/ई + भिन्न स्वर = य; उ/ऊ + भिन्न स्वर = व; ऋ + भिन्न स्वर = र | इति + आदि = इत्यादि; सु + आगत = स्वागत; पितृ + आज्ञा = पित्राज्ञा |
| अयादि | ए, ऐ, ओ, औ + भिन्न स्वर = अय्, आय्, अव्, आव् | ने + अन = नयन; गै + अक = गायक; पो + अन = पवन; पौ + अक = पावक |

**(ख) व्यंजन संधि** (व्यंजन + स्वर/व्यंजन): वाक् + ईश = वागीश; सत् + जन = सज्जन; उत् + ज्वल = उज्ज्वल; सम् + तोष = संतोष; जगत् + नाथ = जगन्नाथ।

**(ग) विसर्ग संधि** (विसर्ग ः + स्वर/व्यंजन): मनः + योग = मनोयोग; निः + धन = निर्धन; दुः + गम = दुर्गम; नमः + ते = नमस्ते; निः + चल = निश्चल।

check.q: 'महोत्सव' में कौन-सी संधि है?
check.why: महा + उत्सव: आ + उ = ओ — यह गुण स्वर संधि है।

sections.md:
दो या अधिक शब्दों के मेल से बने **नए संक्षिप्त शब्द** को **समस्त पद** और इस प्रक्रिया को **समास** कहते हैं। समस्त पद को तोड़ना **समास-विग्रह** है।

| समास | पहचान | उदाहरण (विग्रह) |
|---|---|---|
| **अव्ययीभाव** | पहला पद अव्यय, पूरा पद अव्यय की तरह | यथाशक्ति (शक्ति के अनुसार), प्रतिदिन (हर दिन), आजीवन (जीवन भर) |
| **तत्पुरुष** | दूसरा पद प्रधान; बीच की विभक्ति लुप्त | राजपुत्र (राजा का पुत्र), रसोईघर (रसोई के लिए घर), देशनिकाला (देश से निकाला), हस्तलिखित (हाथ से लिखा) |
| **कर्मधारय** | विशेषण–विशेष्य या उपमान–उपमेय | नीलकमल (नीला है जो कमल), चंद्रमुख (चंद्र के समान मुख), महात्मा (महान है जो आत्मा) |
| **द्विगु** | पहला पद संख्यावाचक, समूह का बोध | चौराहा (चार राहों का समूह), त्रिलोक (तीन लोकों का समूह), सप्ताह (सात दिनों का समूह) |
| **द्वंद्व** | दोनों पद प्रधान; 'और/या' से विग्रह | माता-पिता (माता और पिता), दाल-रोटी, पाप-पुण्य, सुख-दुख |
| **बहुव्रीहि** | दोनों पद अप्रधान; कोई तीसरा अर्थ | दशानन (दस हैं आनन जिसके — रावण), लंबोदर (लंबा है उदर जिसका — गणेश), पीतांबर (पीले हैं अंबर जिसके — कृष्ण), चक्रपाणि (विष्णु) |

**कर्मधारय और बहुव्रीहि का अंतर:** *नीलकंठ* = नीला है जो कंठ (कर्मधारय); नीला है कंठ जिसका — शिव (बहुव्रीहि)। विग्रह से तय होता है।

**द्विगु और बहुव्रीहि:** *त्रिनेत्र* = तीन नेत्रों का समूह (द्विगु); तीन हैं नेत्र जिसके — शिव (बहुव्रीहि)।

check.q: 'दशानन' (रावण) में कौन-सा समास है?
check.why: 'दस हैं आनन जिसके' — दोनों पद मिलकर किसी तीसरे (रावण) का बोध कराते हैं, इसलिए बहुव्रीहि।

sections.md:
**शब्द** जब वाक्य में प्रयुक्त होता है, तो व्याकरण के नियमों में बँधकर **पद** बन जाता है। *राम* शब्द है; *राम ने खाना खाया* में 'राम ने' पद है।

**पदबंध** — जब कई पद मिलकर **एक पद (एक इकाई)** का काम करते हैं, उसे पदबंध कहते हैं। इसमें एक **शीर्ष (मुख्य) पद** होता है, बाकी उसके आश्रित।

| पदबंध | शीर्ष पद | उदाहरण (रेखांकित भाग) |
|---|---|---|
| **संज्ञा पदबंध** | संज्ञा | *चार ताकतवर मज़दूरों ने* बक्सा उठाया। |
| **सर्वनाम पदबंध** | सर्वनाम | *भाग्य की मारी तुम* कहाँ जाओगी? |
| **विशेषण पदबंध** | विशेषण | उसका घर *बहुत सुंदर और बड़ा* है। |
| **क्रिया पदबंध** | क्रिया | वह बाज़ार *जा रहा होगा*। |
| **क्रियाविशेषण पदबंध** | क्रियाविशेषण | वह *बहुत धीरे-धीरे* चल रहा था। |

**पहचान का सूत्र:** पदबंध का अंतिम या मुख्य शब्द देखिए — अगर वह संज्ञा है तो संज्ञा पदबंध; वह किसकी विशेषता बताता है, किस क्रिया को पूरा करता है — यह प्रश्न पूछिए।

- *सुबह से शाम तक* वह पढ़ता रहा — 'कब तक?' → **क्रियाविशेषण पदबंध**।
- *नीली कमीज़ वाला लड़का* मेरा भाई है — शीर्ष 'लड़का' → **संज्ञा पदबंध**।
- बच्चे *खेलते-कूदते चले जा रहे थे* — **क्रिया पदबंध**।

check.q: 'वह लड़का बहुत ही चतुर और परिश्रमी है।' — रेखांकित 'बहुत ही चतुर और परिश्रमी' कौन-सा पदबंध है?
check.why: यह पदसमूह 'लड़का' की विशेषता बताता है, इसलिए विशेषण पदबंध है।

sections.md:
वाक्य में प्रयुक्त पद का **व्याकरणिक परिचय** देना **पद-परिचय** है। हर प्रकार के पद के लिए क्या लिखना है —

| पद | परिचय में लिखें |
|---|---|
| **संज्ञा** | भेद (व्यक्तिवाचक/जातिवाचक/भाववाचक), लिंग, वचन, कारक, क्रिया से संबंध |
| **सर्वनाम** | भेद (पुरुषवाचक, निश्चयवाचक, अनिश्चयवाचक, संबंधवाचक, प्रश्नवाचक, निजवाचक), पुरुष, लिंग, वचन, कारक, क्रिया से संबंध |
| **विशेषण** | भेद (गुणवाचक, संख्यावाचक, परिमाणवाचक, सार्वनामिक), लिंग, वचन, अवस्था, विशेष्य |
| **क्रिया** | भेद (सकर्मक/अकर्मक), लिंग, वचन, पुरुष, काल, वाच्य, कर्ता/कर्म |
| **क्रियाविशेषण** | भेद (कालवाचक, स्थानवाचक, रीतिवाचक, परिमाणवाचक), किस क्रिया की विशेषता |
| **संबंधबोधक / समुच्चयबोधक / विस्मयादिबोधक** | भेद और किन शब्दों/वाक्यों को जोड़ता है या कौन-सा भाव |

**उदाहरण वाक्य:** *मोहन ने कल सुंदर चित्र बनाया।*
- **मोहन ने** — व्यक्तिवाचक संज्ञा, पुल्लिंग, एकवचन, कर्ता कारक, 'बनाया' क्रिया का कर्ता।
- **कल** — कालवाचक क्रियाविशेषण, 'बनाया' क्रिया का काल बताता है।
- **सुंदर** — गुणवाचक विशेषण, पुल्लिंग, एकवचन, विशेष्य 'चित्र'।
- **चित्र** — जातिवाचक संज्ञा, पुल्लिंग, एकवचन, कर्म कारक, 'बनाया' का कर्म।
- **बनाया** — सकर्मक क्रिया, पुल्लिंग, एकवचन, भूतकाल, कर्तृवाच्य; कर्ता 'मोहन', कर्म 'चित्र'।

check.q: 'वह धीरे-धीरे चलता है।' में 'धीरे-धीरे' का पद-परिचय होगा —
options: रीतिवाचक क्रियाविशेषण, 'चलता है' क्रिया की विशेषता
check.why: 'धीरे-धीरे' बताता है कि क्रिया कैसे होती है — यह रीतिवाचक क्रियाविशेषण है।

sections.h: 6. वाक्य भेद — रचना और अर्थ के आधार पर
sections.md:
**(क) रचना के आधार पर:**
| भेद | पहचान | उदाहरण |
|---|---|---|
| सरल | एक समापिका क्रिया | *वर्षा होने पर मोर नाचने लगे।* |
| संयुक्त | स्वतंत्र उपवाक्य + और/पर/या/इसलिए + स्वतंत्र उपवाक्य | *वर्षा हुई और मोर नाचने लगे।* |
| मिश्र | प्रधान + आश्रित (कि, जो, जब, यदि, क्योंकि) | *जब वर्षा हुई, तब मोर नाचने लगे।* |

मिश्र वाक्य के आश्रित उपवाक्य: **संज्ञा** (कि…), **विशेषण** (जो/जिसे…), **क्रियाविशेषण** (जब, जहाँ, क्योंकि, यदि…)।

**(ख) अर्थ के आधार पर आठ भेद:**
| भेद | उदाहरण |
|---|---|
| विधानवाचक | भारत एक विशाल देश है। |
| निषेधवाचक | आज बाज़ार नहीं खुला। |
| प्रश्नवाचक | क्या तुमने खाना खाया? |
| आज्ञावाचक | दरवाज़ा बंद करो। |
| इच्छावाचक | ईश्वर तुम्हें सफलता दे। |
| संदेहवाचक | शायद आज बारिश हो। |
| संकेतवाचक (शर्त) | यदि तुम पढ़ोगे तो पास होगे। |
| विस्मयादिबोधक | वाह! कितना सुंदर दृश्य है! |

**रूपांतरण का नियम:** अर्थ और काल वही रहें, केवल बनावट बदले। *परिश्रमी व्यक्ति सफल होता है* (सरल) → *जो व्यक्ति परिश्रमी होता है, वह सफल होता है* (मिश्र) → *व्यक्ति परिश्रमी होता है और सफल होता है* (संयुक्त)।

check.q: 'शायद वह कल आए।' — अर्थ के आधार पर वाक्य भेद है —
check.why: 'शायद' अनिश्चितता या संदेह प्रकट करता है, इसलिए यह संदेहवाचक वाक्य है।

sections.md:
क्रिया के जिस रूप से पता चले कि वाक्य में **कर्ता, कर्म या भाव** में से किसकी प्रधानता है, वह **वाच्य** है।

| वाच्य | क्रिया किसके अनुसार | उदाहरण |
|---|---|---|
| कर्तृवाच्य | कर्ता (या 'ने' होने पर कर्म) | *सीमा पत्र लिखती है।* |
| कर्मवाच्य | कर्म; कर्ता के साथ 'द्वारा/से'; क्रिया + 'जाना' | *सीमा द्वारा पत्र लिखा जाता है।* |
| भाववाच्य | सदा पुल्लिंग एकवचन; अकर्मक क्रिया; प्रायः 'नहीं' | *सीमा से चला नहीं जाता।* |

**परिवर्तन के चरण (कर्तृ → कर्म):** कर्ता + द्वारा → कर्म प्रधान → मुख्य क्रिया का भूतकालिक रूप + जाना (उसी काल में) → लिंग-वचन कर्म के अनुसार।
- *किसान फसल काट रहे हैं।* → *किसानों द्वारा फसल काटी जा रही है।*
- *मैं नहीं सो सका।* → *मुझसे सोया नहीं जा सका।* (भाववाच्य)

**प्रयोग:** कर्मवाच्य — सूचनाएँ, समाचार, अज्ञात कर्ता (*चोरी की गई*); भाववाच्य — असमर्थता (*मुझसे पढ़ा नहीं जाता*), सुझाव (*चलो, घूमा जाए*)।

sections.md:
काव्य की शोभा बढ़ाने वाले तत्व **अलंकार** हैं। **शब्दालंकार** (शब्द की ध्वनि से चमत्कार) और **अर्थालंकार** (अर्थ से चमत्कार)।

**शब्दालंकार**
| अलंकार | पहचान | उदाहरण |
|---|---|---|
| अनुप्रास | एक वर्ण की बार-बार आवृत्ति | *चारु चंद्र की चंचल किरणें* (च) |
| यमक | एक शब्द बार-बार, **अलग-अलग अर्थ** | *कनक कनक ते सौ गुनी मादकता अधिकाय* (कनक = सोना, धतूरा) |
| श्लेष | एक शब्द एक बार, **अनेक अर्थ** | *पानी गए न ऊबरै मोती मानुष चून* (पानी = चमक, इज़्ज़त, जल) |
| पुनरुक्ति प्रकाश | एक शब्द की आवृत्ति, एक ही अर्थ, भाव पर बल | *घर-घर, धीरे-धीरे, विकल विकल* |

**अर्थालंकार**
| अलंकार | पहचान | उदाहरण |
|---|---|---|
| उपमा | समानता; *सा, सी, से, सम, समान, जैसा* | *पीपर पात सरिस मन डोला* |
| रूपक | उपमेय पर उपमान का अभेद आरोप | *चरण-कमल बंदौं हरि राई* |
| उत्प्रेक्षा | संभावना; *मानो, मनु, जनु, जानो* | *सोहत ओढ़े पीत पट, स्याम सलोने गात। मनौ नीलमनि सैल पर, आतप परयौ प्रभात।* |
| अतिशयोक्ति | बढ़ा-चढ़ाकर वर्णन | *हनुमान की पूँछ में लगन न पाई आग, लंका सिगरी जल गई गए निसाचर भाग।* |
| मानवीकरण | जड़ प्रकृति पर मानवीय भावों का आरोप | *मेघ आए बड़े बन-ठन के सँवर के* |

*(उदाहरण तुलसी, बिहारी, रहीम जैसे प्राचीन कवियों और पारंपरिक उद्धरणों से हैं।)*

check.q: 'मनौ नीलमनि सैल पर आतप परयौ प्रभात' में कौन-सा अलंकार है?
check.why: 'मनौ' (मानो) शब्द से संभावना प्रकट की गई है, इसलिए उत्प्रेक्षा अलंकार है।

sections.md:
काव्य पढ़ने-सुनने से जो **आनंद** मिलता है, वह **रस** है। रस के चार अंग: **स्थायी भाव** (मन में स्थायी रूप से रहने वाला भाव), **विभाव** (भाव जगाने वाले कारण — आलंबन और उद्दीपन), **अनुभाव** (भाव के बाहरी चिह्न — आँसू, रोमांच), **संचारी भाव** (क्षणिक भाव — चिंता, हर्ष)।

| रस | स्थायी भाव | उदाहरण-संकेत |
|---|---|---|
| शृंगार (संयोग/वियोग) | रति (प्रेम) | प्रिय-मिलन या विरह का वर्णन |
| हास्य | हास | विचित्र वेश, वाणी या चेष्टा |
| करुण | शोक | प्रियजन की मृत्यु या विनाश |
| रौद्र | क्रोध | अपमान पर क्रोध — परशुराम का क्रोध |
| वीर | उत्साह | युद्ध या कर्तव्य के लिए उत्साह — 'खूब लड़ी मर्दानी…' |
| भयानक | भय | डरावना दृश्य |
| वीभत्स | जुगुप्सा (घृणा) | घृणित दृश्य |
| अद्भुत | विस्मय | आश्चर्यजनक घटना |
| शांत | निर्वेद | वैराग्य, संसार की नश्वरता |
| वात्सल्य | वत्सलता (संतान-प्रेम) | 'मैया मैं नहिं माखन खायो' (सूरदास) |
| भक्ति | भगवद्-विषयक रति | ईश्वर-भक्ति के पद (मीरा, तुलसी) |

**याद रखें:** काव्यशास्त्र में मूलतः नौ रस माने गए; बाद में **वात्सल्य** और **भक्ति** जोड़े गए, इसलिए कुल 11 रस गिने जाते हैं।

check.q: 'मैया मैं नहिं माखन खायो' में कौन-सा रस है?
check.why: बालक कृष्ण और यशोदा के बीच संतान-स्नेह का भाव है — वात्सल्य रस।

sections.md:
**मुहावरा** — वाक्यांश जो अपना सामान्य अर्थ छोड़कर **विशेष अर्थ** देता है; वाक्य में क्रिया के साथ प्रयोग होता है। **लोकोक्ति** — पूरा वाक्य, लोक-अनुभव पर आधारित कहावत।

| मुहावरा | अर्थ | वाक्य-प्रयोग |
|---|---|---|
| आँखें चार होना | नज़रें मिलना | भीड़ में अचानक हमारी आँखें चार हुईं। |
| आँखों का तारा | बहुत प्यारा | वह अपनी दादी की आँखों का तारा है। |
| आसमान सिर पर उठाना | बहुत शोर करना | शिक्षक के जाते ही बच्चों ने आसमान सिर पर उठा लिया। |
| ईद का चाँद होना | बहुत दिनों बाद दिखना | तुम तो ईद का चाँद हो गए हो! |
| घी के दिए जलाना | ख़ुशियाँ मनाना | जीत की ख़बर पर गाँव में घी के दिए जले। |
| दाँतों तले उँगली दबाना | आश्चर्यचकित होना | जादूगर का खेल देखकर सब दाँतों तले उँगली दबा गए। |
| नाक में दम करना | बहुत परेशान करना | शरारती बंदरों ने नाक में दम कर दिया। |
| पानी-पानी होना | लज्जित होना | झूठ पकड़े जाने पर वह पानी-पानी हो गया। |
| हवा से बातें करना | बहुत तेज़ भागना | राणा का घोड़ा हवा से बातें करता था। |
| हाथ-पाँव फूलना | घबरा जाना | परीक्षा-कक्ष में प्रश्न देखकर उसके हाथ-पाँव फूल गए। |

**लोकोक्तियाँ:** *अधजल गगरी छलकत जाय* (कम ज्ञानी अधिक दिखावा करता है); *नाच न जाने आँगन टेढ़ा* (अपनी कमी का दोष दूसरों पर); *जल में रहकर मगर से बैर* (शक्तिशाली आश्रयदाता से शत्रुता); *अब पछताए होत क्या जब चिड़िया चुग गई खेत* (समय बीतने पर पछताना व्यर्थ)।

check.q: 'पानी-पानी होना' का अर्थ है —
check.why: यह मुहावरा अत्यधिक शर्मिंदगी या लज्जा का भाव प्रकट करता है।

workedExamples.q: संधि-विच्छेद कीजिए और भेद लिखिए: 'स्वागत'
समास-विग्रह कर भेद लिखिए: 'नीलकंठ' (शिव के अर्थ में)
steps: दोनों पद मिलकर तीसरे (शिव) का बोध कराते हैं।

workedExamples.q: पदबंध पहचानिए: 'मेरे सबसे अच्छे मित्र रोहन ने पुरस्कार जीता।'
steps: 'मेरे सबसे अच्छे मित्र रोहन ने' — शीर्ष पद 'रोहन/मित्र' संज्ञा।
यह पूरा समूह कर्ता का काम करता है।

workedExamples.q: पद-परिचय दीजिए: 'वह प्रतिदिन व्यायाम करता है।' — 'वह'
steps: पुल्लिंग (क्रिया 'करता है' से), एकवचन, कर्ता कारक।

rd-school-c10-maths-a.ch1-real-numbers.title: Real Numbers
rd-school-c10-maths-a.ch1-real-numbers.subtitle: Every whole number has a unique prime 'DNA' — and that one fact explains HCF, LCM and why √2 can never be a fraction

keyTerms: prime number — a natural number greater than 1 with exactly two factors, 1 and itself (2, 3, 5, 7, 11…)
composite number — a natural number greater than 1 that has more than two factors
rational number — a number that can be written as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0
irrational number — a real number that cannot be written as p/q

sections.md:
Start with primes and multiply them: 2 × 3 = 6, 2 × 2 × 7 = 28, 3 × 5 × 5 × 11 = 825. By multiplying primes, you can make every composite number. The reverse is also true: every composite number can be **broken down** into primes.

> **Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic:** Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this factorisation is **unique**, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.

So 120 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 2³ × 3 × 5, and there is **no other** set of primes whose product is 120. You might write it as 3 × 2 × 5 × 2 × 2, but the primes and how many times each appears are the same.

**Why 'fundamental'?** Because primes are the 'atoms' of multiplication. In general, a composite number x is written as x = p₁ × p₂ × … × pₙ, where the primes are usually written in **ascending order** (p₁ ≤ p₂ ≤ … ≤ pₙ). Combining equal primes gives powers: 32760 = 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 × 13.

**Did you know?** There are **infinitely many primes**. Euclid proved this around 300 BCE: if there were only finitely many, multiply them all and add 1; the new number is not divisible by any of them, a contradiction. The famous mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss gave one of the first careful proofs of the uniqueness part in 1801.

sections.h: Using the theorem: can 4ⁿ or 6ⁿ end in 0?
sections.md:
A number ends in the digit **0** exactly when it is divisible by 10 = **2 × 5**. So its prime factorisation must contain **both 2 and 5**.

Now 4ⁿ = (2²)ⁿ = 2²ⁿ. Its only prime factor is 2. By the **uniqueness** part of the theorem, there is no other factorisation that could contain 5. Hence **4ⁿ can never end with the digit 0**, for any natural number n.

Similarly 6ⁿ = (2 × 3)ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ contains no 5, so 6ⁿ can never end in 0. But 10ⁿ, 20ⁿ, 15ⁿ × 2 can.

**The same idea for 'composite or prime?' questions.** Is 7 × 11 × 13 + 13 composite? Take out the common factor:
7 × 11 × 13 + 13 = 13 × (7 × 11 + 1) = 13 × 78.
It has factors other than 1 and itself, so it is **composite**.

Is 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 + 5 composite? = 5 × (7 × 6 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 + 1) = 5 × (1008 + 1) = 5 × 1009. **Composite.**

**Pattern to remember:** if a sum has a common factor in every term, factor it out to show the number is composite.

check.q: Why can 12ⁿ never end with the digit 0?
options: Because n is a natural number
check.why: Ending in 0 needs both 2 and 5 as prime factors; 12ⁿ = 2²ⁿ × 3ⁿ contains no 5, and the factorisation is unique.

sections.h: HCF and LCM by prime factorisation
sections.md:
Write each number as a product of prime powers. Then:

- **HCF** = product of the **smallest power** of each **common** prime factor.
- **LCM** = product of the **greatest power** of **each** prime factor that appears in any of the numbers.

**Example: 6 and 20.** 6 = 2¹ × 3¹; 20 = 2² × 5¹.
- Common prime: only 2; smallest power 2¹ → HCF = 2.
- All primes: 2, 3, 5 with greatest powers 2², 3¹, 5¹ → LCM = 4 × 3 × 5 = 60.
- Check: HCF × LCM = 2 × 60 = 120 = 6 × 20 ✔.

**For any two positive integers a and b:**
> HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b

**Why it works:** for each prime, the HCF takes the smaller power and the LCM the larger; together they take both powers — exactly what a × b contains.

**Warning:** this product rule is true for **two** numbers only. For three numbers, in general HCF × LCM ≠ product. Example: 6, 72, 120 → HCF 6, LCM 360; 6 × 360 = 2160, but 6 × 72 × 120 = 51,840.

sections.h: HCF and LCM of three numbers; word problems
sections.md:
**Three numbers: 6, 72 and 120.**
- 6 = 2 × 3
- 72 = 2³ × 3²
- 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5
- HCF: common primes 2 and 3, smallest powers 2¹ and 3¹ → **HCF = 6**.
- LCM: greatest powers 2³, 3², 5¹ → 8 × 9 × 5 = **360**.

**Three numbers: 12, 15 and 21.** 12 = 2² × 3, 15 = 3 × 5, 21 = 3 × 7 → HCF = 3; LCM = 2² × 3 × 5 × 7 = 420.

**Three numbers: 8, 9 and 25.** 8 = 2³, 9 = 3², 25 = 5² → no common prime, so HCF = 1 (they are **co-prime**); LCM = 8 × 9 × 25 = 1800.

**When to use HCF and when LCM in word problems:**
| Clue in the question | Use |
|---|---|
| largest size, greatest number that divides, maximum length of tiles/pieces, arranging in equal rows | **HCF** |
| smallest number divisible by all, when will events coincide again, least time to meet at the start | **LCM** |

**Example (LCM):** At a school sports ground, Sonia takes 18 minutes to complete one round and Ravi takes 12 minutes. They start together at the same point in the same direction. When will they next meet at the starting point? 18 = 2 × 3², 12 = 2² × 3 → LCM = 2² × 3² = 36. They meet again after **36 minutes**.

**Example (HCF):** An army contingent of 616 members marches behind a band of 32 members. Both groups must march in the **same number of columns**. Maximum columns? 616 = 2³ × 7 × 11, 32 = 2⁵ → HCF = 2³ = **8 columns**.

check.q: Two bells ring every 15 and 20 minutes. If they ring together at 9:00 a.m., when will they next ring together?
check.why: LCM(15, 20) = 2² × 3 × 5 = 60 minutes, so they ring together again at 10:00 a.m.

sections.h: 1.3 Revisiting irrational numbers — a key fact
sections.md:
In Class 9 you were told that √2, √3, √5 and π are irrational. Now you can **prove** it. The proofs use one fact that comes from the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic:

> **Theorem 1.2:** Let p be a prime number. If p divides a², then p divides a, where a is a positive integer.

**Proof idea:** let a = p₁ × p₂ × … × pₙ (primes). Then a² = p₁ × p₁ × p₂ × p₂ × … × pₙ × pₙ. If the prime p divides a², then by uniqueness p must be one of the primes in this list, i.e. one of p₁, …, pₙ. But these are exactly the primes of a, so **p divides a**.

Example: 3 divides 36 = 6², and 3 divides 6 ✔. 2 divides 100 = 10², and 2 divides 10 ✔. (Note: this is for **primes**. 4 divides 36 = 6² and 4 does not divide 6 — so the fact can fail for composite p.)

**Proof by contradiction** is the method: assume the opposite of what you want, follow the logic, and reach something impossible. Then the assumption must be false.

**Theorem 1.3:** √2 is irrational.

**Proof (by contradiction).**
1. Assume √2 is rational. Then we can find integers a and b (b ≠ 0) such that √2 = a/b.
2. If a and b have a common factor other than 1, divide it out, so we may assume **a and b are co-prime** (HCF = 1).
3. Then b√2 = a. Squaring: **2b² = a²**. So 2 divides a².
4. By Theorem 1.2 (2 is prime), **2 divides a**. So write a = 2c for some integer c.
5. Substitute: 2b² = (2c)² = 4c², so **b² = 2c²**. Hence 2 divides b², and therefore **2 divides b**.
6. Now 2 divides both a and b — this **contradicts** the fact that a and b are co-prime.
7. The contradiction arose from the assumption that √2 is rational. Hence **√2 is irrational**. ∎

The same proof, with 3 in place of 2, shows **√3 is irrational**: assume √3 = a/b (co-prime) → 3b² = a² → 3 | a → a = 3c → b² = 3c² → 3 | b → contradiction. And likewise **√5**, **√7**, and √p for any prime p.

check.q: In the proof that √2 is irrational, what is contradicted?
options: That a and b are co-prime
check.why: The proof shows 2 divides both a and b, contradicting the assumption that a/b was in lowest terms (a and b co-prime).

sections.md:
These use a neat fact: **rational ± rational, rational × rational and rational ÷ (non-zero) rational are all rational**. So if a combination with √3 were rational, √3 itself would be rational — a contradiction.

**Example: prove that 5 − √3 is irrational.**
1. Assume 5 − √3 is rational: 5 − √3 = a/b, with a, b co-prime integers, b ≠ 0.
2. Rearranging: √3 = 5 − a/b = (5b − a)/b.
3. Since a and b are integers, (5b − a)/b is rational. So √3 would be rational.
4. This contradicts the fact that √3 is irrational. Hence 5 − √3 is irrational. ∎

**Example: prove that 3√2 is irrational.**
1. Assume 3√2 = a/b (co-prime, b ≠ 0).
2. Then √2 = a/(3b), which is rational.
3. Contradiction, since √2 is irrational. Hence 3√2 is irrational. ∎

**Example: prove that 1/√2 is irrational.** Assume 1/√2 = a/b → √2 = b/a (a ≠ 0), rational — contradiction.

**Example: 6 + √2.** Assume 6 + √2 = a/b → √2 = a/b − 6 = (a − 6b)/b, rational — contradiction.

**Did you know?** The sum of two irrationals need not be irrational: (2 + √3) + (2 − √3) = 4. And √2 × √2 = 2. That is why every proof must be written carefully — you cannot just say 'irrational plus anything is irrational'. It is true that **rational + irrational = irrational** and **non-zero rational × irrational = irrational**, which is what these proofs use.

check.q: Which of these is rational?
check.why: √2 × √8 = √16 = 4, which is rational; the others are rational ± or × an irrational, hence irrational.

sections.h: Summary of the chapter and common mistakes
sections.md:
**What this chapter proves:**
1. Every composite number factorises into primes uniquely (apart from order).
2. HCF = product of smallest powers of common primes; LCM = product of greatest powers of all primes.
3. For two positive integers, HCF × LCM = product.
4. If a prime p divides a², then p divides a.
5. √2, √3, √5 (and √p, p prime) are irrational; so are numbers like 5 − √3, 3√2, 1/√2.

**Common mistakes:**
- Writing 1 as a prime in a factorisation. (1 is neither prime nor composite.)
- Using HCF × LCM = product for **three** numbers.
- Forgetting to state 'a and b are co-prime' in an irrationality proof — the whole contradiction depends on it.
- Saying '2 divides a², so a² is even, so a is even' **without** justification — cite Theorem 1.2.
- In word problems, mixing up HCF (largest equal parts) and LCM (next meeting time).

**Exam tip:** in 'Is it composite?' questions, always **factor out** the common term and show the product; a bare 'yes' scores nothing.

summary: Real numbers = rational numbers (p/q, q ≠ 0) + irrational numbers.
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every composite number is a product of primes, uniquely apart from order.

If a prime p divides a², then p divides a.

Rational + irrational is irrational; non-zero rational × irrational is irrational.

rd-school-c10-maths-a.ch2-polynomials.subtitle: Where a curve crosses the x-axis — and the secret link between zeroes and coefficients

sections.md:
Virat lofts a ball towards the boundary at the Wankhede. Its height above the ground, in metres, t seconds after the hit, is roughly h(t) = −5t² + 20t + 1. When does the ball land? That is the same as asking: **for which t is h(t) = 0?** Those values are called the **zeroes** of the polynomial. This chapter is about zeroes: how to *see* them on a graph, and how they are secretly tied to the numbers (coefficients) that make up the polynomial.

### Quick recap from Class 9
A **polynomial** in x is an expression like 3x² − 5x + 2, made of terms a·xⁿ where n is a whole number (0, 1, 2, …). The highest power of x is the **degree**.

| Degree | Name | General form |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | linear | ax + b, a ≠ 0 |
| 2 | quadratic | ax² + bx + c, a ≠ 0 |
| 3 | cubic | ax³ + bx² + cx + d, a ≠ 0 |

Expressions like 1/x or √x + 2 are *not* polynomials (negative and fractional powers are not allowed).

The **value** of p(x) at x = k is p(k), found by substitution. If p(k) = 0, then k is a **zero** of p(x). For p(x) = x² − 3x − 4: p(4) = 16 − 12 − 4 = 0, and p(−1) = 1 + 3 − 4 = 0. So 4 and −1 are the zeroes.
keyTerms: Degree — highest power of the variable
Zero of p(x) — a number k with p(k) = 0
Coefficient — the number multiplying a power of x

check.q: What is the degree of 5x³ − 4x² + x − 2?
check.why: The highest power of x present is x³, so the degree is 3 and the polynomial is cubic.

sections.md:
Draw the graph y = p(x). A point lies on the x-axis exactly when y = 0. So:

> **The zeroes of p(x) are the x-coordinates of the points where the graph of y = p(x) meets the x-axis.**

**Linear, y = 2x + 3:** a straight line crossing the x-axis once, at x = −3/2. A linear polynomial ax + b has exactly **one** zero, −b/a.

**Quadratic, y = x² − 3x − 4:** the graph is a **parabola**. Since a = 1 > 0 it opens upwards like a cup. It meets the x-axis at (−1, 0) and (4, 0). A quadratic's graph can do one of three things:

1. Cut the x-axis at **two** distinct points → two zeroes.
2. **Touch** the x-axis at exactly one point → one (repeated) zero. Example: y = x² − 4x + 4 = (x − 2)², touching at x = 2.
3. **Miss** the x-axis completely → no real zero. Example: y = x² + 1, which is always at least 1.

If a < 0 the parabola opens downwards (like the path of Virat's ball), but the same three cases apply.

**Cubic:** a cubic graph can meet the x-axis 1, 2 or 3 times — never 0 times, because it must go from very negative to very positive (or the reverse). For y = x³ − 4x = x(x − 2)(x + 2), the zeroes are −2, 0, 2.

> **General rule: a polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes.** A graph of degree n can cross the x-axis at most n times.

check.why: A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes, so three zeroes require degree at least 3.

sections.h: Zeroes and coefficients of a quadratic
sections.md:
Here is the secret link. Take p(x) = 2x² − 8x + 6. Factorise by splitting the middle term: 2x² − 2x − 6x + 6 = 2x(x − 1) − 6(x − 1) = 2(x − 1)(x − 3). Zeroes: α = 1, β = 3.

Now compare with the coefficients a = 2, b = −8, c = 6:
- α + β = 4, and −b/a = 8/2 = 4. ✔
- αβ = 3, and c/a = 6/2 = 3. ✔

This is always true. If α and β are zeroes of ax² + bx + c, then ax² + bx + c = a(x − α)(x − β) = a x² − a(α + β)x + aαβ. Matching coefficients:

> **α + β = −b/a = −(coefficient of x)/(coefficient of x²)**
> **αβ = c/a = (constant term)/(coefficient of x²)**

### Example
p(x) = x² + 7x + 10 = (x + 2)(x + 5). Zeroes −2, −5. Sum = −7 = −7/1 ✔. Product = 10 = 10/1 ✔.

p(x) = 3x² − x − 4 = (3x − 4)(x + 1). Zeroes 4/3 and −1. Sum = 1/3 = −(−1)/3 ✔. Product = −4/3 = −4/3 ✔.

### Going backwards: build a quadratic from its zeroes
If you know S = α + β and P = αβ, a quadratic with these zeroes is

> **k[x² − Sx + P]**, for any non-zero constant k.

Example: sum −3, product 2 → x² + 3x + 2. Sum 1/4, product −1 → x² − ¼x − 1, or (multiplying by 4) 4x² − x − 4.

> Did you know? The Indian mathematician Brahmagupta (7th century CE) gave rules for solving quadratic equations — including negative quantities, which many European mathematicians resisted for centuries afterwards.
keyTerms: α + β = −b/a
αβ = c/a
Quadratic from zeroes: x² − (sum)x + (product)

check.q: Find a quadratic polynomial whose zeroes have sum √2 and product 1/3.
check.why: x² − √2x + 1/3, multiplied by 3, gives 3x² − 3√2x + 1, whose zeroes have sum √2 and product 1/3.

sections.md:
For a cubic ax³ + bx² + cx + d with zeroes α, β, γ, the same matching gives:

- α + β + γ = −b/a
- αβ + βγ + γα = c/a
- αβγ = −d/a

**Check with p(x) = 2x³ − 5x² − 14x + 8.** Try x = 4: 128 − 80 − 56 + 8 = 0 ✔. Try x = −2: −16 − 20 + 28 + 8 = 0 ✔. Try x = ½: 2(⅛) − 5(¼) − 7 + 8 = ¼ − 1¼ + 1 = 0 ✔. Zeroes 4, −2, ½.

- Sum = 4 − 2 + ½ = 5/2 and −b/a = 5/2 ✔
- Pairwise: (4)(−2) + (−2)(½) + (½)(4) = −8 − 1 + 2 = −7 and c/a = −14/2 = −7 ✔
- Product = 4 × (−2) × ½ = −4 and −d/a = −8/2 = −4 ✔

The current NCERT syllabus focuses on quadratics for examinations, but this pattern shows the idea is general and beautiful: the coefficients of any polynomial are built from symmetric combinations of its zeroes.

check.q: For a cubic with zeroes 1, 2, 3 and leading coefficient 1, what is the constant term?
check.why: αβγ = −d/a gives 6 = −d, so d = −6; indeed (x−1)(x−2)(x−3) = x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6.

sections.h: Strategy: finding zeroes in exam questions
sections.md:
Most exam questions on this chapter follow a recipe:

1. **Factorise** the quadratic by splitting the middle term (find two numbers whose product is ac and sum is b).
2. **Set each factor to zero** to get the zeroes.
3. **Verify** the relations α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a.

**Splitting the middle term, slowly:** 6x² − 7x − 3. Here ac = 6 × (−3) = −18, b = −7. Two numbers with product −18 and sum −7: −9 and 2. So 6x² − 9x + 2x − 3 = 3x(2x − 3) + 1(2x − 3) = (2x − 3)(3x + 1). Zeroes 3/2 and −1/3. Sum = 7/6 = −(−7)/6 ✔; product = −1/2 = −3/6 ✔.

**When there's no constant term:** 4u² + 8u = 4u(u + 2). Zeroes 0 and −2. Sum −2 = −8/4 ✔, product 0 = 0/4 ✔.

**When there's no x term:** t² − 15 = (t − √15)(t + √15). Zeroes ±√15. Sum 0 = −0/1 ✔, product −15 ✔.

**Using the relations without finding zeroes:** if α, β are zeroes of x² − 5x + 6, find α² + β². Use α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 25 − 12 = 13. (Check: zeroes are 2 and 3; 4 + 9 = 13 ✔.)

| Expression | In terms of S = α+β, P = αβ |
|---|---|
| α² + β² | S² − 2P |
| 1/α + 1/β | S/P |
| (α − β)² | S² − 4P |

check.q: If α, β are zeroes of x² − 6x + 4, what is 1/α + 1/β?

workedExamples.q: Find the zeroes of x² + 7x + 10 and verify the relationship with coefficients.
Find the zeroes of 4s² − 4s + 1.
Find a quadratic polynomial whose zeroes are 3 and −5.
Find the zeroes of 3x² − x − 4.
If one zero of 2x² + kx − 6 is 2, find k and the other zero.

summary: A polynomial's degree is its highest power; linear (1), quadratic (2), cubic (3).
k is a zero of p(x) if p(k) = 0.
Zeroes are the x-coordinates where y = p(x) meets the x-axis.
Linear ax + b has one zero, −b/a.
A quadratic's parabola meets the x-axis in 2, 1 or 0 points.
Parabola opens up if a > 0, down if a < 0.
A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes.
For ax² + bx + c: α + β = −b/a, αβ = c/a.
Quadratic with given sum S and product P: k(x² − Sx + P).
Cubic: α+β+γ = −b/a, αβ+βγ+γα = c/a, αβγ = −d/a.
Use α² + β² = S² − 2P and 1/α + 1/β = S/P to avoid solving.
practice: Find the zeroes of x² − 2x − 8 and verify the relationship between zeroes and coefficients.
Find the zeroes of 6x² − 3 − 7x and verify the relationship.
Find a quadratic polynomial whose zeroes have sum −1/4 and product 1/4.
Find a quadratic polynomial whose zeroes are 2 + √3 and 2 − √3.
How many zeroes can a cubic polynomial have? Draw rough sketches for each case.
If α and β are zeroes of x² − 5x + k and α − β = 1, find k.
If α, β are zeroes of 2x² − 5x + 3, find α² + β².
Explain, with a sketch, why y = x² + 4 has no real zeroes.

rd-school-c10-maths-a.ch2-polynomials-2.title: Polynomials — Part 2: Every exercise type, graphs, division and exam craft
rd-school-c10-maths-a.ch2-polynomials-2.subtitle: Reading zeroes off any graph, every Exercise 2.1–2.2 pattern, the division algorithm and the traps examiners set

sections.md:
Part 1 gave you the big ideas. Part 2 walks through the chapter **in textbook order** and makes sure no type of question can surprise you.

| NCERT section | What it is about | Where in this read |
|---|---|---|
| 2.1 Introduction | Recap: polynomial, degree, value, zero | Part 1 §1 and below |
| 2.2 Geometrical meaning of zeroes | Zeroes = x-intercepts of the graph | Part 1 §2, Part 2 §2 |
| Exercise 2.1 | Count zeroes from six graphs | Part 2 §2 |
| 2.3 Relationship between zeroes and coefficients | α + β = −b/a, αβ = c/a; cubic version | Part 1 §3–4, Part 2 §3–4 |
| Exercise 2.2 | Find zeroes and verify; build quadratics from sum and product | Part 2 §3–4 |
| Division algorithm (older editions / enrichment) | p(x) = g(x)q(x) + r(x) | Part 2 §5 |
| 2.4 Summary | Key results | Summary list |

### A quick recap of the vocabulary
- A **term** is a number times a whole-number power of x: 7x³, −2x, 5 (that last one is 5x⁰).
- A **constant polynomial** is just a number, like 4. Its degree is 0. The **zero polynomial** 0 has no defined degree.
- **Monomial, binomial, trinomial**: one, two or three terms.
- In ax² + bx + c, a is the **leading coefficient** and c is the **constant term**.

Why does this matter? Because the relations between zeroes and coefficients only work if you read a, b and c correctly. A huge number of exam mistakes come from rearranging the polynomial carelessly. Always rewrite it first in **standard form** (descending powers). For example, 6x² − 3 − 7x must be rewritten as 6x² − 7x − 3, so a = 6, b = −7, c = −3 — not b = −3.

> Did you know? The word *polynomial* mixes Greek *poly* (many) with Latin *nomen* (name/term). Mathematicians have grumbled about the hybrid for 400 years, but the word stuck.
keyTerms: Standard form — terms written in descending powers
Leading coefficient — coefficient of the highest power
Constant polynomial — degree 0, e.g. 7

check.q: In 5 − 2x + 3x², what is b?
check.why: In standard form the polynomial is 3x² − 2x + 5, so a = 3, b = −2 and c = 5.

sections.h: Exercise 2.1 style: counting zeroes from a graph
sections.md:
In this exercise you are shown graphs of y = p(x) and asked only one thing: **how many zeroes does p(x) have?** You do not need the formula of the polynomial. You just count how many times the curve **meets** the x-axis — crossing or touching both count.

Work through these six typical shapes:

1. **A horizontal-ish line never touching the axis** (e.g. y = 3 drawn above the axis): 0 zeroes.
2. **A straight slanted line**: exactly 1 zero.
3. **A U-shaped parabola that dips below the axis**: 2 zeroes.
4. **A parabola whose lowest point sits on the axis**: 1 zero (a repeated zero).
5. **A wiggly curve that crosses three times**: 3 zeroes.
6. **A curve that crosses once and touches once**: 2 distinct zeroes.

Three traps to avoid:
- **Meeting the y-axis does not count.** The y-intercept is p(0), the constant term. It tells you nothing about zeroes unless it happens to be at the origin.
- **A curve that crosses at the origin** has 0 as a zero. Count it!
- **Don’t assume degree from the count.** If you see 2 crossings, the degree could be 2, or 4, or any even/odd number ≥ 2. The graph only proves degree ≥ number of zeroes.

### Why a quadratic can never have 3 zeroes
If a quadratic had three zeroes r, s, t, it would have three factors (x − r), (x − s), (x − t), which multiply to an x³ term. Contradiction. In general degree n ⇒ at most n zeroes.

### Why a cubic always has at least one
For large positive x, the ax³ term dominates, so if a > 0 the graph shoots up; for large negative x it plunges down. A continuous curve going from below the axis to above must cross it at least once. That is why the count for a cubic is always 1, 2 or 3.

check.q: A graph passes through (0, 0), crosses the x-axis again at x = 3 and never meets it elsewhere. How many zeroes?
check.why: The origin lies on the x-axis, so x = 0 is a zero, and x = 3 is the second zero, giving 2 zeroes.

sections.h: Exercise 2.2 type A: find zeroes and verify — six patterns
sections.md:
Every question of this type has three steps: **factorise, read off zeroes, verify both relations.** The factorising is where marks are lost, so here is one example of each pattern you will meet.

**Pattern 1 — all positive:** x² + 9x + 20. Product 20, sum 9 → 4 and 5. (x + 4)(x + 5). Zeroes −4, −5. Sum −9 = −9/1 ✔. Product 20 ✔.

**Pattern 2 — negative middle, positive end:** x² − 9x + 14. Product 14, sum −9 → −2 and −7. (x − 2)(x − 7). Zeroes 2, 7. Sum 9 = −(−9)/1 ✔. Product 14 ✔.

**Pattern 3 — negative end:** x² + x − 12. Product −12, sum 1 → 4 and −3. (x + 4)(x − 3). Zeroes −4, 3. Sum −1 ✔. Product −12 ✔.

**Pattern 4 — leading coefficient not 1:** 8x² − 22x − 21. ac = −168, b = −22 → −28 and 6. 8x² − 28x + 6x − 21 = 4x(2x − 7) + 3(2x − 7) = (2x − 7)(4x + 3). Zeroes 7/2, −3/4. Sum = 14/4 − 3/4 = 11/4 = 22/8 ✔. Product = −21/8 ✔.

**Pattern 5 — missing constant (u-variable):** 5u² + 10u = 5u(u + 2). Zeroes 0, −2. Sum −2 = −10/5 ✔. Product 0 = 0/5 ✔.

**Pattern 6 — difference of squares with irrational zeroes:** x² − 7 = (x − √7)(x + √7). Zeroes ±√7. Sum 0 ✔. Product −7 ✔.

### The *repeated zero* pattern
4x² − 12x + 9 = (2x − 3)². Zeroes 3/2, 3/2. Sum 3 = 12/4 ✔. Product 9/4 ✔. Write the zero *twice* when verifying.

### How to find the two numbers fast
List factor pairs of |ac|. If ac > 0 the two numbers have the **same sign** as b. If ac < 0 they have **opposite signs**, and the bigger one (in size) takes the sign of b. For ac = −168, b = −22: pairs of 168 are (1,168), (2,84), (3,56), (4,42), (6,28), (7,24), (8,21), (12,14). Difference 22 → (6, 28), so −28 and +6.

check.q: The zeroes of x² − 2x − 8 are:
check.why: x² − 2x − 8 = (x − 4)(x + 2), so the zeroes are 4 and −2; their sum 2 equals −b/a and product −8 equals c/a.

sections.h: Exercise 2.2 type B: build the quadratic — and harder twists
sections.md:
Here you are given the sum S and product P and must write a quadratic. Use **x² − Sx + P**, then clear fractions by multiplying by a convenient k.

| Given S, P | x² − Sx + P | Neat form |
|---|---|---|
| ¼, −1 | x² − ¼x − 1 | 4x² − x − 4 |
| √2, ⅓ | x² − √2x + ⅓ | 3x² − 3√2x + 1 |
| 0, √5 | x² + √5 | x² + √5 |
| 1, 1 | x² − x + 1 | (has no real zeroes!) |
| −¼, ¼ | x² + ¼x + ¼ | 4x² + x + 1 |
| 4, 1 | x² − 4x + 1 | x² − 4x + 1 |

Notice the row S = 1, P = 1: the recipe still produces a valid polynomial even though its graph never meets the x-axis. The relations hold for complex zeroes too, which you will meet in Class 11.

### Twist 1: zeroes given directly
Zeroes 2 + √3 and 2 − √3: S = 4, P = 4 − 3 = 1 → x² − 4x + 1.

### Twist 2: find an unknown coefficient
If the zeroes of x² − 5x + k differ by 1: (α − β)² = S² − 4P ⇒ 1 = 25 − 4k ⇒ k = 6. Check: x² − 5x + 6 has zeroes 2 and 3 ✔.

If one zero of kx² + 3x − 2 is the reciprocal of the other: product = 1 ⇒ −2/k = 1 ⇒ k = −2.

If the sum of zeroes of 3x² − (3k − 2)x − (k − 6) equals their product: (3k − 2)/3 = −(k − 6)/3 ⇒ 3k − 2 = −k + 6 ⇒ k = 2.

### Twist 3: a new quadratic from old zeroes
If α, β are zeroes of x² − 3x + 2, find a quadratic with zeroes 2α and 2β. New S = 2(α + β) = 6; new P = 4αβ = 8 → x² − 6x + 8. Check: original zeroes 1, 2; doubled 2, 4; (x − 2)(x − 4) = x² − 6x + 8 ✔.
keyTerms: (α − β)² = S² − 4P
Reciprocal zeroes ⇒ product = 1 ⇒ c = a
Opposite zeroes ⇒ sum = 0 ⇒ b = 0

check.q: If the zeroes of ax² + bx + c are negatives of each other, then:
check.why: If β = −α then α + β = 0 = −b/a, which forces b = 0.

sections.h: The division algorithm (enrichment from older editions)
sections.md:
Earlier editions of this chapter also taught how to **divide one polynomial by another**, just like long division of numbers. It is still useful: it lets you find all zeroes of a cubic once you know one of them.

> **Division algorithm:** for polynomials p(x) and g(x) ≠ 0, there are polynomials q(x) and r(x) with **p(x) = g(x) × q(x) + r(x)**, where r(x) = 0 or degree r < degree g.

Compare with numbers: 17 = 5 × 3 + 2.

### Worked long division
Divide p(x) = 3x³ + x² + 2x + 5 by g(x) = x² + 2x + 1.
1. 3x³ ÷ x² = **3x**. Multiply: 3x³ + 6x² + 3x. Subtract: −5x² − x + 5.
2. −5x² ÷ x² = **−5**. Multiply: −5x² − 10x − 5. Subtract: 9x + 10.
3. Degree of 9x + 10 is 1 < 2, stop.

q(x) = 3x − 5, r(x) = 9x + 10. **Check:** (x² + 2x + 1)(3x − 5) = 3x³ − 5x² + 6x² − 10x + 3x − 5 = 3x³ + x² − 7x − 5; add 9x + 10 → 3x³ + x² + 2x + 5 ✔.

### Using a known zero
If 2 is a zero of x³ − 3x² − x + 3... first test: 8 − 12 − 2 + 3 = −3 ≠ 0, so 2 is *not* a zero. Try 1: 1 − 3 − 1 + 3 = 0 ✔. Divide by (x − 1): x³ − 3x² − x + 3 = (x − 1)(x² − 2x − 3) = (x − 1)(x − 3)(x + 1). Zeroes 1, 3, −1. Sum 3 = −(−3)/1 ✔; product −3 = −3/1 ✔.

### Checking whether one polynomial is a factor
g(x) is a factor of p(x) exactly when the remainder is 0. E.g. x² − 3 is a factor of 2x⁴ + 3x³ − 2x² − 9x − 12, because division gives quotient 2x² + 3x + 4 and remainder 0. (Verify: (x² − 3)(2x² + 3x + 4) = 2x⁴ + 3x³ + 4x² − 6x² − 9x − 12 ✔.)

> Did you know? Computer algebra systems like those used by engineers do millions of polynomial divisions a second to simplify the equations that describe aircraft wings and electrical circuits.

sections.h: Common mistakes, exam strategy and a marking guide
sections.md:
### Ten mistakes examiners see every year
1. Reading b from an un-arranged polynomial (6x² − 3 − 7x).
2. Writing the sum as +b/a instead of −b/a.
3. Forgetting to verify both relations when the question says *verify*.
4. Losing a repeated zero (writing only ‘3/2’ instead of ‘3/2, 3/2’).
5. Treating x = 0 as ‘no zero’ in polynomials with no constant term.
6. Counting y-axis meetings in graph questions.
7. Writing a quadratic from zeroes as x² + Sx + P (sign error).
8. Sloppy fraction arithmetic when verifying: always use a common denominator.
9. Saying a quadratic ‘has no zeroes’ when it has a repeated one.
10. Claiming the graph shows the exact degree.

### How marks are usually split (typical 3-mark question)
- 1 mark: correct factorisation.
- ½ mark: zeroes stated.
- 1½ marks: both relations verified with working.

### A 60-second self-check routine
After finding zeroes, plug one back in. For 8x² − 22x − 21 at x = 7/2: 8(49/4) − 22(7/2) − 21 = 98 − 77 − 21 = 0 ✔. Ten seconds that can save three marks.

### Linking to other chapters
- **Chapter 4 (Quadratic Equations)** uses exactly these zeroes as *roots* of ax² + bx + c = 0, and adds the quadratic formula and discriminant b² − 4ac, which tells you in advance whether the parabola cuts, touches or misses the axis.
- **Chapter 3 (Linear equations)** is about graphs of degree-1 polynomials meeting each other.
- In physics, the cricket-ball equation h(t) = −5t² + 20t + 1 is a quadratic; its positive zero (about t = 4.05 s) is when the ball lands.

rd-school-c10-maths-a.ch3-linear-equatio.title: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rd-school-c10-maths-a.ch3-linear-equatio.subtitle: Two lines, one answer: how to solve two clues at once — by graph, by substitution, by elimination

sections.md:
At a Pune mela, Akhila spends ₹20 on rides: 3 on the Giant Wheel and some on Hoopla. Her brother says, 'You took half as many Giant Wheel rides as Hoopla games, and each ride costs ₹3 and each Hoopla game ₹4 — so you spent ₹20.' Can you find how many of each she had?

One clue alone is not enough: '3x + 4y = 20' has endless solutions if fractions are allowed. But two clues *together* can pin down a single answer. Let x = number of rides, y = number of Hoopla games.

- Clue 1: x = y/2, i.e. **x − ½y = 0** (or y = 2x)
- Clue 2: **3x + 4y = 20**

Substitute y = 2x: 3x + 8x = 20 → x = 20/11 — not a whole number! So the brother's story is inconsistent with whole rides. Let's fix the story: suppose instead the rides cost ₹3 each and Hoopla ₹4, she had **twice as many Hoopla games as rides** and spent ₹22. Then 3x + 8x = 22 → x = 2, y = 4. Two rides, four Hoopla games. ✔

This is exactly what the chapter is about: a **pair of linear equations in two variables**,

> a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 and a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0,

where a, b, c are real numbers and a² + b² ≠ 0 for each. A **solution** is a pair (x, y) that makes *both* true at once.
keyTerms: Linear equation in two variables — ax + by + c = 0
Solution of a pair — values satisfying both equations
Consistent — has at least one solution

check.q: Is (2, 4) a solution of the pair 3x + 4y = 22 and y = 2x?
check.why: 3(2) + 4(4) = 22 and 4 = 2 × 2, so (2, 4) satisfies both equations at once.

sections.h: The graphical method: where lines meet
sections.md:
Each linear equation in two variables is a **straight line** on the Cartesian plane — every point on the line is a solution of that equation. A solution of the pair must lie on *both* lines. Two lines in a plane can behave in only three ways:

1. **Intersect at one point** → exactly **one** solution. The pair is *consistent*.
2. **Parallel (never meet)** → **no** solution. The pair is *inconsistent*.
3. **Coincident (the same line)** → **infinitely many** solutions. The pair is *dependent* (and consistent).

### Drawing an example
Solve x + y = 5 and x − y = 1 graphically. Make a small table for each:

| x + y = 5 | x: 0, 5, 2 | y: 5, 0, 3 |
|---|---|---|
| x − y = 1 | x: 1, 0, 3 | y: 0, −1, 2 |

Plot and join. The lines cross at **(3, 2)**. Check: 3 + 2 = 5 ✔, 3 − 2 = 1 ✔.

### Reading the ratios — without drawing
Compare the coefficients:

| Condition | Lines | Solutions |
|---|---|---|
| a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂ | intersecting | exactly one |
| a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂ | parallel | none |
| a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂ | coincident | infinitely many |

Example: x − 2y = 0 and 3x + 4y − 20 = 0: a₁/a₂ = 1/3, b₁/b₂ = −2/4 = −½. Unequal → one solution.
Example: 2x + 3y = 9 and 4x + 6y = 18: ratios 2/4 = 3/6 = 9/18 = ½ → coincident.
Example: x + 2y = 4 and 2x + 4y = 12: ratios ½ = ½ ≠ 4/12 = ⅓ → parallel, no solution.

sections.md:
Graphs are wonderful for *seeing*, but if the answer is (1.37, −2.08) you can't read it accurately from paper. Algebra gives exact answers.

**Substitution, in three steps:**
1. From one equation, express one variable in terms of the other (pick the easiest — a coefficient of 1 helps).
2. Substitute into the *other* equation, giving one equation in one variable. Solve it.
3. Put the value back to get the second variable. Check in both originals.

**Example:** 7x − 15y = 2 and x + 2y = 3.
- From the second: x = 3 − 2y.
- Substitute: 7(3 − 2y) − 15y = 2 → 21 − 14y − 15y = 2 → −29y = −19 → **y = 19/29**.
- x = 3 − 38/29 = (87 − 38)/29 = **49/29**.
- Check in first: 7(49/29) − 15(19/29) = (343 − 285)/29 = 58/29 = 2 ✔.

**What substitution reveals about special cases.** Solve 2x + 3y = 9 and 4x + 6y = 18. From the first, x = (9 − 3y)/2. Substitute: 4(9 − 3y)/2 + 6y = 18 → 18 − 6y + 6y = 18 → 18 = 18. A statement true for *all* y! That signals infinitely many solutions (coincident lines).

If instead you reach something like 0 = 5 — always false — the lines are parallel and there is **no** solution.

check.q: While solving a pair by substitution you get 9 = 4. What does this mean?
options: No solution — the lines are parallel
You must have made an arithmetic error
check.why: A false statement with no variables left means no (x, y) can satisfy both equations, so the lines are parallel.

sections.md:
Sometimes it is cleaner to **add or subtract** the equations so one variable vanishes.

**Steps:**
1. Multiply one or both equations by suitable non-zero numbers so the coefficients of one variable become equal (or opposite).
2. Subtract (or add) to eliminate that variable.
3. Solve, back-substitute, check.

**Example:** The ratio of incomes of two people is 9 : 7 and the ratio of their expenditures is 4 : 3. Each saves ₹2000 per month. Find their incomes.

Let incomes be 9x and 7x, expenditures 4y and 3y.
- 9x − 4y = 2000 … (1)
- 7x − 3y = 2000 … (2)

Multiply (1) by 3 and (2) by 4: 27x − 12y = 6000 and 28x − 12y = 8000. Subtract: x = 2000. So incomes are **₹18,000 and ₹14,000**. (Check: y from (1): 18000 − 4y = 2000 → y = 4000; expenditures ₹16,000 and ₹12,000; savings 2000 each ✔.)

**Which method should I use?**
- A variable has coefficient 1 or −1 → substitution is quick.
- Coefficients are 'nice' multiples of each other → elimination.
- Asked to 'solve graphically' → draw it, and still check algebraically.

> Did you know? Solving many linear equations at once is what computers do when they forecast monsoons, design bridges, or route Indian Railways' freight — some systems have millions of variables, but the idea is the same elimination you learn here.

left.title: Substitution
points: Natural for word problems with 'x = …' clues

right.title: Elimination
points: Add or subtract to remove a variable
Best with symmetric or big coefficients

check.q: To eliminate y from 3x + 4y = 10 and 2x − 2y = 2, you could:
options: Multiply the second by 2 and add
Multiply the first by 2 and subtract
check.why: 2 × (2x − 2y = 2) gives 4x − 4y = 4, and adding to 3x + 4y = 10 cancels y to give 7x = 14, so x = 2.

sections.h: Word problems: turning stories into equations
sections.md:
Most marks in this chapter come from translating a story into two equations. A reliable routine:

1. **Name the unknowns** clearly: 'Let the cost of one pen be ₹x and one pencil be ₹y.'
2. **Write one equation per clue.**
3. **Solve** by any method.
4. **Answer in words with units**, and check it makes sense (no negative people!).

### Common patterns
| Story type | Typical setup |
|---|---|
| Ages | 'Five years hence' → (x + 5), 'five years ago' → (x − 5) |
| Two-digit numbers | Number = 10x + y; reversed = 10y + x |
| Fractions | x/y; 'add 1 to numerator' → (x + 1)/y |
| Speed of boats | downstream speed = u + v, upstream = u − v |
| Fixed + variable charge | Total = fixed + rate × quantity |
| Rectangles | perimeter, area changes |

**Example (fixed + variable):** A library charges a fixed amount for the first 3 days and then a fixed amount per extra day. Saritha paid ₹27 for 7 days, Susy ₹21 for 5 days. Let fixed charge = x, per extra day = y.
- x + 4y = 27, x + 2y = 21. Subtract: 2y = 6 → y = 3, x = 15.
Fixed charge **₹15**, extra **₹3 per day**.

**Example (digits):** The sum of a two-digit number and the number obtained by reversing its digits is 66, and the digits differ by 2. (10x + y) + (10y + x) = 66 → x + y = 6, with x − y = 2 → x = 4, y = 2: the number **42** (or 24 if y − x = 2). Both work!

check.q: A boat goes 30 km upstream in 3 h and 30 km downstream in 2 h. If u = boat speed in still water and v = stream speed, which pair is correct?
check.why: Upstream speed u − v = 30/3 = 10 km/h and downstream speed u + v = 30/2 = 15 km/h, giving u = 12.5 and v = 2.5 km/h.

story.title: Chai, Samosa and the Missing Bill

parts.md: The canteen at Nikhil's school in Lucknow lost its rate card in the rain. Nikhil remembered that on Monday his group paid ₹70 for 2 chais and 3 samosas, and on Tuesday ₹55 for 3 chais and 1 samosa... no, wait, 1 chai and 3 samosas? He frowned. 'If I misremember the second bill, I'll get a nonsense answer.' He wrote: 2c + 3s = 70 and c + 3s = 55. Subtracting: c = 15. Then 3s = 40 — not a whole rupee. 'Something's off.' He asked the canteen uncle, who laughed: 'Tuesday was 3 chais and 2 samosas for ₹65.'

Now: 2c + 3s = 70, 3c + 2s = 65. Multiply the first by 3 and the second by 2: 6c + 9s = 210 and 6c + 4s = 130. Subtract: 5s = 80, s = 16, so 2c = 70 − 48 = 22, c = 11. 'Chai ₹11, samosa ₹16.' Uncle nodded. Check Tuesday: 33 + 32 = 65 ✔. Nikhil grinned — two clues, one truth, and a lesson that a wrong clue shows up as a strange answer.

summary: General form: a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0, a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0.
Each equation is a straight line; a solution lies on both lines.
Intersecting lines → one solution (consistent).
Parallel lines → no solution (inconsistent).
Coincident lines → infinitely many solutions (dependent, consistent).
a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂ → unique solution.
a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂ → no solution.
a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂ → infinitely many.
Substitution: isolate, substitute, solve, back-substitute.
Elimination: equalise coefficients, add/subtract, solve.
A true identity (like 0 = 0) means infinitely many solutions; a false one (like 0 = 3) means none.
Always check your answer in both original equations.

sections.h: Map of the chapter in textbook order
sections.md:
This part is your complete companion to the chapter, section by section.

| NCERT section | Idea | Exercise |
|---|---|---|
| 3.1 Introduction | Two unknowns, two conditions | — |
| 3.2 Graphical method | Draw both lines; read where they meet | Ex 3.1 |
| 3.3 Algebraic methods | — | — |
| 3.3.1 Substitution | Express one variable, substitute | Ex 3.2 |
| 3.3.2 Elimination | Make coefficients equal, add or subtract | Ex 3.3 |
| Older editions: cross-multiplication, equations reducible to linear form | Enrichment | — |
| 3.4 Summary | — | — |

A **linear equation in two variables** has the form ax + by + c = 0 with a and b not both zero. Its graph is a **straight line**, and every point on that line is a solution. A **pair** of such equations asks: which (x, y) satisfies *both*? Geometrically: where do the two lines meet?

> Hook: At a mela in Jaipur, Akhila spends ₹20 on rides and games together. A ride costs ₹3 and a game ₹4, and she takes twice as many rides as games. How many of each? One unknown can't capture this neatly — you need two unknowns and two conditions. That is the whole chapter in one sentence.

check.q: Which of these is NOT a linear equation in two variables?
check.why: xy = 6 contains the product of the variables (degree 2), so its graph is a curve, not a straight line.

sections.h: 3.2 The graphical method, step by step
sections.md:
**Recipe.**
1. For each equation, find two or three solutions and put them in a small table.
2. Plot the points and join them into a line (a third point catches arithmetic slips).
3. Read off the intersection and check it in both equations.

**Example (Akhila).** Let rides = x and games = y. Twice as many rides as games: x = 2y, i.e. x − 2y = 0. Money: 3x + 4y = 20.

| x − 2y = 0 | (0, 0) | (2, 1) | (4, 2) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **3x + 4y = 20** | **(0, 5)** | **(4, 2)** | **(20/3, 0)** |

Both tables contain (4, 2), so the lines meet there: **4 rides and 2 games**. Check: 12 + 8 = 20 ✔ and 4 = 2 × 2 ✔.

### Three possible pictures
| Picture | Number of solutions | Name |
|---|---|---|
| Lines intersect at one point | exactly one | consistent |
| Lines coincide (same line) | infinitely many | consistent, dependent |
| Lines are parallel | none | inconsistent |

### Typical Exercise 3.1 tasks
- **Form the pair and solve graphically**, e.g. ‘10 students took part in a quiz; girls were 4 more than boys’: x + y = 10, x − y = 4 → girls 7, boys 3.
- **Pencils and pens**: 5 pencils + 7 pens = ₹50, 7 pencils + 5 pens = ₹46 → pencil ₹3, pen ₹5 (check 15 + 35 = 50 ✔, 21 + 25 = 46 ✔).
- **Find the vertices of a triangle** formed by two lines and the x-axis: e.g. x − y + 1 = 0 and 3x + 2y − 12 = 0 meet at (2, 3); they cut the x-axis at (−1, 0) and (4, 0). Shading that triangle is a favourite graph question.
- **Write a second equation** so the pair is intersecting / parallel / coincident (see the ratio test next).

check.why: Parallel lines never meet, so no point lies on both and the pair is inconsistent.

sections.h: The ratio test: knowing the picture without drawing
sections.md:
For a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 and a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0, compare the ratios:

| Condition | Lines | Solutions |
|---|---|---|
| a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂ | intersecting | unique |
| a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂ | coincident | infinitely many |
| a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂ | parallel | none |

**Why it works:** equal a/b ratios mean equal slopes (−a/b), so the lines are parallel or the same; then the c ratio decides whether they are the same line.

**Examples.**
- 5x − 4y + 8 = 0, 7x + 6y − 9 = 0: 5/7 vs −4/6 → unequal → intersecting.
- 9x + 3y + 12 = 0, 18x + 6y + 24 = 0: 9/18 = 3/6 = 12/24 = ½ → coincident.
- 6x − 3y + 10 = 0, 2x − y + 9 = 0: 6/2 = −3/−1 = 3, but 10/9 ≠ 3 → parallel.

**Finding k.** For which k does kx + 3y = k − 3, 12x + ky = k have no solution? Need k/12 = 3/k → k² = 36 → k = ±6, and also 3/k ≠ (k − 3)/k. For k = 6: 3/6 vs 3/6 — equal, so coincident, reject. For k = −6: 3/(−6) = −½ vs (−9)/(−6) = 3/2 — unequal ✔. **k = −6.**

**Writing a partner equation.** Given 2x + 3y − 8 = 0: intersecting partner 3x − 2y − 7 = 0; parallel partner 4x + 6y − 9 = 0; coincident partner 6x + 9y − 24 = 0.
keyTerms: Consistent — at least one solution
Inconsistent — no solution
Dependent — infinitely many (coincident lines)

check.q: x + 2y = 4 and 2x + 4y = 12 are:
check.why: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = ½ but c₁/c₂ = 4/12 = ⅓, so the lines are parallel and the pair has no solution.

sections.h: 3.3.1 Substitution — and the intext question types
sections.md:
**Recipe.** (1) From one equation, write one variable in terms of the other. (2) Substitute into the other equation; solve the one-variable equation. (3) Back-substitute. (4) Check.

**Example.** 7x − 15y = 2 and x + 2y = 3. From the second, x = 3 − 2y. Then 7(3 − 2y) − 15y = 2 → 21 − 29y = 2 → y = 19/29. x = 3 − 38/29 = 49/29. Check: 7(49/29) − 15(19/29) = (343 − 285)/29 = 58/29 = 2 ✔.

**What substitution reveals.** If the variable cancels and you get a *true* statement (like 9 = 9), the pair has infinitely many solutions. If you get a *false* one (like 0 = 7), there is no solution.

Example: 2x + 3y = 9, 4x + 6y = 18. y = (9 − 2x)/3. Substituting: 4x + 2(9 − 2x) = 18 → 18 = 18. Always true → infinitely many solutions (coincident lines).

**Exercise 3.2 also asks**: ‘solve, then find m such that y = mx + 3’. Solve 2x + 3y = 11 and 2x − 4y = −24: subtract → 7y = 35 → y = 5, x = −2. Then 5 = −2m + 3 → m = −1.

**Age problem (classic).** Five years hence, the father’s age will be three times the son’s; five years ago, father was seven times the son. Let father x, son y. x + 5 = 3(y + 5) → x − 3y = 10. x − 5 = 7(y − 5) → x − 7y = −30. Subtract: 4y = 40 → y = 10, x = 40.

check.q: While substituting, you reach 0 = 5. The pair is:
check.why: A false statement with no variable left means no (x, y) can satisfy both equations, so the pair is inconsistent.

sections.md:
**Recipe.** (1) Multiply the equations by suitable numbers so one variable has equal (or opposite) coefficients. (2) Subtract (or add) to eliminate it. (3) Solve, back-substitute, check.

**Example.** 3x + 4y = 10 and 2x − 2y = 2. Multiply the second by 2: 4x − 4y = 4. Add: 7x = 14 → x = 2; then 2(2) − 2y = 2 → y = 1. Check: 6 + 4 = 10 ✔.

**Example with fractions.** x/2 + 2y/3 = −1 and x − y/3 = 3. Clear denominators: 3x + 4y = −6 and 3x − y = 9. Subtract: 5y = −15 → y = −3, x = 2.

**Symmetric trick.** 99x + 101y = 499 and 101x + 99y = 501. Add: 200(x + y) = 1000 → x + y = 5. Subtract: −2x + 2y = −2 → y − x = −1. So x = 3, y = 2.

### Which method when?
| Situation | Best method |
|---|---|
| A variable has coefficient 1 | substitution |
| Coefficients are easy multiples | elimination |
| You need to *see* the solution or vertices | graphical |
| Coefficients swapped (ax + by, bx + ay) | add and subtract |

### Enrichment: cross-multiplication
For a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0, a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0 with a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ ≠ 0:
x = (b₁c₂ − b₂c₁)/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁), y = (c₁a₂ − c₂a₁)/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁).
For 2x + 3y − 8 = 0, 4x + 5y − 14 = 0: denominator 10 − 12 = −2; x = (3(−14) − 5(−8))/(−2) = (−42 + 40)/(−2) = 1; y = ((−8)(4) − (−14)(2))/(−2) = (−32 + 28)/(−2) = 2. Check 2 + 6 = 8 ✔.

### Enrichment: equations reducible to linear form
2/x + 3/y = 13, 5/x − 4/y = −2. Put p = 1/x, q = 1/y: 2p + 3q = 13, 5p − 4q = −2 → p = 2, q = 3 → x = ½, y = ⅓.

sections.md:
Nearly every word problem belongs to one of these families. Learn the set-up and the rest is algebra.

1. **Costs** — ‘2 bats and 1 ball cost ₹… ’: price × quantity sums.
2. **Ages** — shift both ages by the same years ‘hence’ or ‘ago’.
3. **Digits** — a two-digit number with tens digit x, units y is 10x + y; reversed is 10y + x. Example: sum of digits 9, and 9 times the number = twice the reversed number: x + y = 9, 90x + 9y = 20y + 2x → 88x = 11y → y = 8x → x = 1, y = 8. Number 18 (check 9 × 18 = 162 = 2 × 81 ✔).
4. **Fractions** — numerator x, denominator y: ‘add 1 to both and it becomes ½’ gives 2(x + 1) = y + 1.
5. **Geometry** — angles of a triangle sum to 180°, supplementary angles sum to 180°, opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, rectangle perimeters and areas.
6. **Fixed + variable charges** — taxi fare, hostel mess, library fine: total = fixed + rate × units. Example: library charges a fixed fee for 3 days then ₹ per extra day; Saritha pays ₹27 for 7 days, Susy ₹21 for 5 days: x + 4y = 27, x + 2y = 21 → y = 3, x = 15.
7. **Speed and boats/trains** — speed = distance/time; downstream speed = boat + stream, upstream = boat − stream.

**Set-up checklist:** define both variables in words with units; translate each sentence into one equation; solve; answer in a full sentence with units; check against the original story (not just your equations).

> Did you know? The ancient Chinese text *Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art* (around 2,000 years ago) solved systems of linear equations with counting rods using a method essentially the same as modern elimination.

check.q: A two-digit number has tens digit x and units digit y. The number obtained by reversing its digits is:
check.why: Reversing puts y in the tens place and x in the units place, so the value is 10y + x.

workedExamples.q: The cost of 2 kg apples and 1 kg grapes was ₹160; a month later 4 kg apples and 2 kg grapes cost ₹300. Is there a consistent price pair?
steps: Ratios a,b equal, c different → parallel lines
workedExamples.answer: No solution if prices were unchanged — the prices must have changed.

summary: A pair of linear equations represents two straight lines.
Intersecting → unique solution; coincident → infinitely many; parallel → none.
Ratio test: a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂ unique; all three equal → infinite; a,b equal but c different → none.
Graphical method: two or three points per line, plot, read intersection, check.
Substitution: express one variable, substitute, back-substitute.
Elimination: equalise one coefficient, add or subtract.
A true constant statement (8 = 8) means infinitely many solutions; false (0 = 3) means none.
Swapped coefficients: add and subtract the equations.
Cross-multiplication (enrichment) gives x and y directly by formula.
Equations in 1/x, 1/y become linear with p = 1/x, q = 1/y.

rd-school-c10-maths-a.ch4-quadratic-equa.title: Quadratic Equations
rd-school-c10-maths-a.ch4-quadratic-equa.subtitle: From prayer halls to cricket balls: solving ax² + bx + c = 0 and reading the discriminant

sections.md:
A charity trust wants to build a rectangular prayer hall with a carpet area of 300 m², and its length should be one metre more than twice its breadth. What should the breadth be? Let the breadth be x metres. Then length = 2x + 1, and

x(2x + 1) = 300, i.e. **2x² + x − 300 = 0**.

This is a **quadratic equation**: an equation of the form

> **ax² + bx + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers and a ≠ 0.**

In Chapter 2 you found the *zeroes of a quadratic polynomial*; the **roots** of the quadratic equation are exactly those zeroes. A real number α is a root of ax² + bx + c = 0 if aα² + bα + c = 0.

### Is it quadratic?
Always simplify first. (x + 2)³ = x³ − 4 expands to x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8 = x³ − 4, i.e. 6x² + 12x + 12 = 0 — quadratic, because the x³ terms cancel! (x − 2)² + 1 = 2x − 3 gives x² − 6x + 8 = 0, also quadratic. But x(x + 1) + 8 = (x + 2)(x − 2) gives x + 12 = 0 — *not* quadratic (linear).

> Did you know? Babylonian clay tablets from around 2000 BCE solve problems equivalent to quadratics, and Indian mathematicians Brahmagupta (628 CE) and Sridharacharya gave general methods. Sridharacharya's rule is essentially the formula you will learn below.

check.q: Which of these is a quadratic equation?
check.why: x(2x + 3) = x² + 1 simplifies to x² + 3x − 1 = 0, which has a ≠ 0; the other three all simplify to linear equations.

sections.md:
If a product is zero, at least one factor is zero. So if we can write ax² + bx + c as a product of two linear factors, the roots appear instantly.

**Split the middle term:** find two numbers whose **product is ac** and whose **sum is b**.

**Example: 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0.** ac = 6, b = −5 → numbers −2 and −3. 2x² − 2x − 3x + 3 = 2x(x − 1) − 3(x − 1) = (2x − 3)(x − 1). Roots **x = 3/2, x = 1**.

**Example: 6x² − x − 2 = 0.** ac = −12, b = −1 → numbers −4 and 3. 6x² + 3x − 4x − 2 = 3x(2x + 1) − 2(2x + 1) = (3x − 2)(2x + 1). Roots **2/3, −1/2**.

**Example: 3x² − 2√6x + 2 = 0.** ac = 6, b = −2√6 → numbers −√6 and −√6. 3x² − √6x − √6x + 2 = √3x(√3x − √2) − √2(√3x − √2) = (√3x − √2)². Root **√2/√3 = √(2/3)**, repeated.

### Back to the prayer hall
2x² + x − 300 = 0. ac = −600, b = 1 → numbers 25 and −24. 2x² + 25x − 24x − 300 = x(2x + 25) − 12(2x + 25) = (2x + 25)(x − 12). Roots −25/2 and 12. A breadth can't be negative, so **breadth = 12 m, length = 25 m**. Check: 12 × 25 = 300 ✔.

That last step matters: in word problems, always **reject** roots that make no physical sense.

check.q: The roots of x² − 3x − 10 = 0 are:
check.why: x² − 5x + 2x − 10 = (x − 5)(x + 2), so the roots are 5 and −2; check: 25 − 15 − 10 = 0.

sections.h: Completing the square and the quadratic formula
sections.md:
Factorising is fast, but not every quadratic splits nicely. **Completing the square** always works, and it leads to a formula.

**Example: 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0.** Divide by 2: x² − (7/2)x + 3/2 = 0. Half of 7/2 is 7/4, so add and subtract (7/4)²:
(x − 7/4)² − 49/16 + 24/16 = 0 → (x − 7/4)² = 25/16 → x − 7/4 = ±5/4 → **x = 3 or ½**.

### Deriving the formula
Do the same for ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0):
- Divide by a: x² + (b/a)x + c/a = 0.
- Complete the square: (x + b/2a)² = (b² − 4ac)/4a².
- If b² − 4ac ≥ 0, take square roots: x + b/2a = ±√(b² − 4ac)/2a.

> **x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] / 2a**

This is the **quadratic formula** (Sridharacharya's rule). It solves *every* quadratic equation that has real roots.

**Example: 3x² − 5x + 2 = 0.** a = 3, b = −5, c = 2; b² − 4ac = 25 − 24 = 1. x = (5 ± 1)/6 → **1 or 2/3**.

**Example: x² + 4x − 5 = 0.** b² − 4ac = 16 + 20 = 36. x = (−4 ± 6)/2 → **1 or −5**.

**Example: x² − 2x − 1 = 0.** b² − 4ac = 4 + 4 = 8. x = (2 ± 2√2)/2 = **1 ± √2** — irrational roots that factorisation would never have found by guessing.

check.q: Using the formula, the roots of x² − 6x + 7 = 0 are:

sections.md:
Look again at the formula. Everything depends on the quantity under the square root:

> **D = b² − 4ac, the discriminant** — it 'discriminates' between kinds of roots.

| D | Roots | Graph of y = ax² + bx + c |
|---|---|---|
| D > 0 | two distinct real roots | cuts x-axis at two points |
| D = 0 | two equal real roots, x = −b/2a | touches x-axis at one point |
| D < 0 | no real roots | doesn't meet the x-axis |

**Examples.**
- 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0: D = 16 − 24 = −8 < 0 → no real roots.
- 2x² − 6x + 3 = 0: D = 36 − 24 = 12 > 0 → two distinct real roots (3 ± √3)/2.
- 9x² − 6x + 1 = 0: D = 36 − 36 = 0 → equal roots 1/3, 1/3.

**Finding k for equal roots.** For 2x² + kx + 3 = 0 to have equal roots, D = k² − 24 = 0 → **k = ±2√6**.

**Is it possible?** Can a rectangular mango grove whose length is twice its breadth have area 800 m²? 2x² = 800 → x = 20 m, length 40 m — yes. Can two friends' ages sum to 20 years with the product of their ages four years ago equal to 48? Let one age be x: (x − 4)(16 − x) = 48 → x² − 20x + 112 = 0, D = 400 − 448 < 0 → **not possible**. The discriminant tells you a story is impossible before you solve anything!

keyTerms: Root — value satisfying the equation
Discriminant D = b² − 4ac
Equal roots — D = 0, x = −b/2a

check.q: For what value of k does kx(x − 2) + 6 = 0 have equal roots?
check.why: kx² − 2kx + 6 = 0 has D = 4k² − 24k = 4k(k − 6) = 0, and k = 0 is rejected because the equation would not be quadratic, leaving k = 6.

sections.h: Word problems that lead to quadratics
sections.md:
Quadratics appear whenever two unknown quantities are **multiplied** — area, product of numbers, speed × time, price × quantity.

**Consecutive numbers:** find two consecutive positive integers whose squares sum to 365. x² + (x + 1)² = 365 → 2x² + 2x − 364 = 0 → x² + x − 182 = 0 → (x + 14)(x − 13) = 0. Take **13 and 14** (169 + 196 = 365 ✔).

**Speed and time:** a train travels 360 km at uniform speed. If the speed were 5 km/h more, it would take 1 hour less. Speed x: 360/x − 360/(x + 5) = 1 → 360 × 5 = x(x + 5) → x² + 5x − 1800 = 0 → (x + 45)(x − 40) = 0. **Speed 40 km/h** (check: 9 h at 40, 8 h at 45 ✔).

**Cottage industry:** a craftsman makes x toys a day, costing (55 − x) rupees each, with total cost ₹750. x(55 − x) = 750 → x² − 55x + 750 = 0 → (x − 25)(x − 30) = 0. **25 or 30 toys** — both valid!

**A tip:** when a problem has fractions like 1/x, multiply through by the LCM of the denominators carefully, and always write the final quadratic in standard form before solving.

> Did you know? The path of a thrown ball, the shape of a satellite dish, and the curve of car headlight reflectors are all parabolas — the graphs of quadratics.

check.q: A train covers 360 km; 5 km/h faster it would take 1 h less. Which equation models this (speed x)?
check.why: Time at the slower speed minus time at the faster speed equals 1 hour, giving 360/x − 360/(x + 5) = 1.

workedExamples.q: Solve 100x² − 20x + 1 = 0.

> Hook: A rectangular prayer hall in Varanasi must have area 300 m², and its length is one metre more than twice its breadth. What are the dimensions? Let the breadth be x: x(2x + 1) = 300, i.e. **2x² + x − 300 = 0**. One clean equation, but to solve it you need the tools of this chapter.

### A little history
Babylonian clay tablets (around 4,000 years ago) solve problems that amount to quadratics. In India, the *Sulba Sutras* involve such constructions, and **Brahmagupta** (598–c.668 CE) stated a rule equivalent to the formula for ax² + bx = c. **Sridharacharya** (around 9th–10th century CE) gave the method of completing the square that leads to the modern formula; it is often called Sridharacharya’s formula in India. Al-Khwarizmi (around 820 CE) also treated quadratics systematically.

check.q: Which of these is a quadratic equation?
check.why: (x − 2)² + 1 = 2x − 3 simplifies to x² − 6x + 8 = 0, degree 2; in the other three the x² terms cancel, leaving linear equations.

sections.md:
An equation is quadratic only after you **simplify fully** and the highest surviving power is 2.

- (x + 1)² = 2(x − 3) → x² + 2x + 1 = 2x − 6 → x² + 7 = 0 ✔ quadratic.
- x² − 2x = (−2)(3 − x) → x² − 2x = −6 + 2x → x² − 4x + 6 = 0 ✔.
- (x − 2)(x + 1) = (x − 1)(x + 3) → x² − x − 2 = x² + 2x − 3 → −3x + 1 = 0 ✘ linear (x² cancels).
- (x − 3)(2x + 1) = x(x + 5) → 2x² − 5x − 3 = x² + 5x → x² − 10x − 3 = 0 ✔.
- x³ − 4x² − x + 1 = (x − 2)³ → x³ − 4x² − x + 1 = x³ − 6x² + 12x − 8 → 2x² − 13x + 9 = 0 ✔ — the cubes cancel, so it *is* quadratic!
- (x + 2)³ = x³ − 4 → x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8 = x³ − 4 → 6x² + 12x + 12 = 0 ✔ also quadratic.

### Forming equations from situations (Ex 4.1, Q2 type)
1. **Area:** a plot of 528 m² with length one more than twice the breadth: x(2x + 1) = 528 → 2x² + x − 528 = 0.
2. **Consecutive integers:** product of two consecutive positive integers is 306: x(x + 1) = 306 → x² + x − 306 = 0.
3. **Ages:** Rohan’s mother is 26 years older; product of their ages 3 years from now is 360: (x + 3)(x + 29) = 360 → x² + 32x − 273 = 0.
4. **Speed:** a train covers 480 km; 8 km/h slower would take 3 h longer: 480/(x − 8) − 480/x = 3 → 3x² − 24x − 3840 = 0 → x² − 8x − 1280 = 0.

Check item 4: 480x − 480(x − 8) = 3x(x − 8) → 3840 = 3x² − 24x ✔.

check.q: The product of two consecutive positive integers is 306. If the smaller is x, the equation is:
check.why: x(x + 1) = 306 rearranges to x² + x − 306 = 0.

sections.md:
**Principle:** if A × B = 0 then A = 0 or B = 0. So factorise ax² + bx + c into two linear factors and set each to zero. The solutions are called **roots**; they are the zeroes of the polynomial ax² + bx + c from Chapter 2.

**Splitting the middle term:** find two numbers with product ac and sum b.

| Equation | ac, b | Split | Roots |
|---|---|---|---|
| x² − 3x − 10 = 0 | −10, −3 | −5, 2 | 5, −2 |
| 2x² + x − 6 = 0 | −12, 1 | 4, −3 | −2, 3/2 |
| √2x² + 7x + 5√2 = 0 | 10, 7 | 5, 2 | −5/√2, −√2 |
| 2x² − x + ⅛ = 0 (×8: 16x² − 8x + 1) | 16, −8 | −4, −4 | ¼, ¼ |
| 100x² − 20x + 1 = 0 | 100, −20 | −10, −10 | 1/10, 1/10 |

Working for the surd case: √2x² + 5x + 2x + 5√2 = x(√2x + 5) + √2(√2x + 5) = (√2x + 5)(x + √2). ✔

**Solving the hook:** 2x² + x − 300 = 0. ac = −600, b = 1 → 25 and −24. 2x² + 25x − 24x − 300 = x(2x + 25) − 12(2x + 25) = (2x + 25)(x − 12). x = 12 (breadth can’t be −12.5). **Hall: 12 m by 25 m.** Check 12 × 25 = 300 ✔.

**Rejecting roots:** in word problems, always discard roots that make no physical sense (negative lengths, speeds, ages, or non-integers where integers are needed) — and say why.
